articles.title_orig: Nvidia Stock Rises Despite Wall Street’s First Call for CEO Huang to Step Down
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Stock Rises Despite Wall Street’s First Call for CEO Huang to Step Down
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock rose close to 5% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.
Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.
Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.
Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.
In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings.
In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.
Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.
"It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.
— CNBC's Michael Bloom and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: Iran vows not to part with "single particle of enriched nuclear material" as standoff continues
articles.content_orig:
Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif called for dialogue and restraint to ease regional tensions during a meeting Wednesday with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, according to Sharif's office.
Sharif expressed deep concern over the prolonged conflict as the two spoke on the sidelines of the United Nations climate summit in Turkey, his office said. The prime minister stressed the need to build on an interim deal reached between the U.S. and Iran in June.
In August, Pezeshkian described the deal as the best way for Iran to move on from a situation that he described as "neither war nor peace."
President Trump said Wednesday the U.S. has already won the war against Iran, but when the conflict will end is a different question.
"America did not start a war with Iran," he said at a Veterans Day event at Arlington National Cemetery in Virginia. "Iran has been waging war on America since 1979. This should have been taken care of a long time ago."
"Under this administration, and it was about time, somebody fought back," he continued. "All of us fought back. We fought back. And we seriously fought back. And we won. Just a question of when we want to end it. We want to make sure we have a total victory, not a 93% victory. It's going to be total. It'll take them 25 years to rebuild back what we have destroyed, and hopefully we won't have to destroy any more of that country."
The president reminded Americans that the Korean War lasted much longer and cost more lives, as did the Vietnam War and the Iraq War.
As he has been saying for months, Mr. Trump said the conflict will be over soon.
Iranian security chief Mohsen Rezaei threatened to strike U.S. bases beyond the Middle East, including in Europe, if they are used for attacks against the Islamic Republic.
"If American aircraft take off from an American military base, even one located in a European country or some other distant region, to bomb Iran, we will strike those bases as well," Rezaei told Lebanon-based Al Mayadeen TV in an interview broadcast Wednesday.
In a "60 Minutes" interview that aired Sunday, President Trump said he does not currently see "any reason" to escalate the war.
Rezaei also said that Iran's response to renewed U.S. attacks would "target America's more distant military installations — including the ones we have not yet attacked," without specifying.
"We may even strike certain islands that they assume are beyond the reach of our missiles," he added during the interview, which was conducted in Tehran.
The Saudi-led coalition fighting Yemen's Houthis said on Wednesday that it shot down three cruise missiles fired at Riyadh, which has been targeted for weeks by the Iran-backed group.
"Air defenses intercepted and destroyed 3 cruise missiles launched by the Houthi terrorist militia toward the Riyadh area," coalition spokesperson Turki al-Malki posted on social media.
The latest incident comes after the Houthis damaged a skyscraper belonging to oil giant Saudi Aramco in the capital's gleaming financial district on Sunday.
Riyadh's international airport has also been targeted repeatedly, with deadly attacks forcing it to close for two weeks last month.
Saudi Arabia formed an international coalition to fight the Houthis in 2015, after the group's takeover of Yemen's capital Sanaa.
After years of an uneasy truce, the conflict reignited in July.
Iran's Defense Ministry on Wednesday rejected Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's latest blustery assessment of Tehran's military capacities, calling his depiction a fabrication and insisting Iranian armed forces still had weapons stockpiled.
Iran's weapons stockpile "far exceeds the deceptive figures fabricated by Trump and the defeated Pete," a ministry spokesperson said, adding that the country had made use of "strategic production and upgraded technologies."
Hegseth told reporters Tuesday that during 40 days of combat, the U.S. had struck 13,000 targets, destroying, he said, more than 80% of Iran's nuclear industrial base.
"Their navy sunk, their air force grounded, their defense industrial base gone," Hegseth said.
Iranian officials claimed a month ago that the country's weapons production capacity had increased by 250% since the war began, with help from Russia and China.
Neither side has offered evidence to prove their claims, and neither the U.S. nor Iran have launched large-scale strikes since the summer. Both claim to have won the war, but despite Hegseth's assertion on Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz is under U.S. control, Iran continues attacking vessels daily in and near the waterway.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has relocated from his home in the Washington, D.C., area to a military base following a series of Iranian threats against his life.
"The secretary will not be deterred by the Iranian regime's threats and remains committed to executing Operation Economic Outcast and maintaining the blockade, which together are collapsing Iran's economy," a Treasury Department spokesperson said.
A source familiar with the situation pointed to a Wall Street Journal story as the impetus for the move.
"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety," the person told CBS News.
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian accused the U.S. on Wednesday of threatening to attack his country with America's largest non-nuclear weapon — the "mother of all bombs" — while claiming to seek a diplomatic resolution to the war.
In a post on X , Pezeshkian criticized the U.S. for what he called an effort to "pursue diplomacy through threats."
"No contradiction but a disgrace. Who threatens global peace and security?" he wrote.
CBS News reported in October that the White House and Pentagon had prepared plans to use the Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb, or MOAB — an acronym that has earned it the nickname used by Pezeshkian —   to hit military sites in Iran if President Trump were to give the order, according to sources familiar with the matter.
The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear weapon in the U.S. arsenal, weighing upwards of 30,000 pounds. Mr. Trump set a precedent for its use in 2017, when it was deployed to attack an ISIS cave complex in Afghanistan. It is designed to destroy infrastructure buried deep underground.
An adviser to Iran's supreme leader said Wednesday that the U.S. and Europe "have heard the repercussions" of the war launched jointly more than eight months ago by the U.S. and Israel.
In a post on X, Mohammad Mokhber said other nations' participation in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports constituted an act of war that would be recorded "in the nation's historical memory."
"Responsibility and the consequences of such actions will extend to all participants, regardless of geographical boundaries," Mokhber said.
He did not mention any specific repercussions, but France has blamed Iran for nationwide cyberattacks that hit commercial refrigeration units at hundreds of grocery stores in October, spoiling thousands of tons of food and causing at least 20 fires, according to French prosecutors.
In September, U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Iran was believed to have "played a part" in a security incident near an air base in England that had been used by U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran.
Iran-linked groups have also been accused of backing a series of sabotage attacks in the U.K. and Europe, including many targeting Jewish communities.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said Wednesday that two more oil tankers had struck sea mines and caught on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, the latest of what have become daily claims by Iranian forces about attacks on commercial vessels in and around the strategic waterway.

articles.title_zh: Watch: Acquitted 'China spy' Chris Cash speaks to BBC
articles.content_orig:
A British man who was acquitted of spying for China has told the BBC he was a "convenient fall guy" for UK police and security services who wanted to put espionage threats by foreign states "on the map".
Chris Cash, a former parliamentary researcher, has shared more than 6,000 messages with us, revealing how a Chinese official sought information about sensitive political matters in the UK - including the 2022 Tory leadership battle to decide the next prime minister.
In his first interview since his acquittal, which sparked a political row over the government's failure to designate China as a "threat", Cash admits he was "unprofessional and naive" to send "gossiping" texts to his friend, Chris Berry, who was in China at the time.
Berry, who was also acquitted of espionage, declined to comment on this story, but previously denied any wrongdoing and said he had been "unfairly subjected to a trial by media".
The BBC's politics investigations correspondent Joe Pike speaks to Cash about the allegations.

articles.title_orig: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
articles.title_zh: Big Walk used AI to fix a bug. Now the indie gaming world is having a reckoning.
articles.content_orig:
The last few years have seen significant debate over the widespread use of AI-powered tools in game development and the responsible disclosure of that usage to players. That debate has exploded into a full-blown controversy in the indie game development space this week, as Big Walk developer House House has publicly and belatedly disclosed minimal AI use in its popular co-operative puzzle exploration game.
This particular controversy has been brewing behind the scenes for months, as judges and jury members for the prestigious Independent Games Festival Awards discussed the issue in private discussion groups. But the debate started to break into public view on Monday when 19 members of the 50-plus-member jury released a signed statement outlining a stance “declining to vote for any game that uses generative AI in any capacity.”
Noting “a significant increase in the number of submitted games developer with generative AI tools,” the group of jurors called out AI’s ecological, economic, psychological, and labor harms in rejecting tools whose use, they said, is still “not a foregone conclusion in our industry.”
The jurors also urged the IGF as a whole to “adopt a strong anti-AI policy for future years that disallows games containing any AI-generated work.”
Although the jurors’ statement didn’t name any specific games, by Tuesday morning, one critical darling in particular was increasingly being noted as a central part of the debate. In a statement provided to Aftermath (and added to the game’s FAQ page shortly thereafter), developer House House admitted publicly that “LLMs were used sparingly” near the end of Big Walk ‘s development “to help work through some difficult technical challenges and bugs.”
That limited AI use—which House House says represents “well under 0.1% of Big Walk ‘s code—stemmed in part from a thorny Unity engine bug that was slowing the game down with “infinite length” shadows during some game situations. After consulting with a Unity engineer who determined a fix “wasn’t possible,” House House said it consulted an LLM chatbot, which suggested a possible fix that the developers “had to modify… extensively” into the 10 lines of code that ended up in the final game ( At least one social media user says the bug was indeed fixable with significant human effort, though).
House House said it didn’t disclose this LLM usage for Big Walk ‘s Steam release earlier this year because Valve “does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” Indeed, Valve’s AI disclosure form for developers specifically notes that it is concerned with AI-generated content, not “efficiency gains” from “modern game development environments [that] have AI powered tools built into them.”
The IGF Awards make no such distinction for AI usage, however, which led House House to mention its AI-assisted bug fix in submitting the game for awards consideration. A version of that disclosure is being made public now because “it has become a matter of public interest,” House House said.
“This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House wrote. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalization of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable.’ We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologize that Big Walk ’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.”
Learning of House House’s AI disclosure was particularly painful for some IGF judges who had previously felt a special connection to Big Walk . In a blog post discussing his feelings , IGF jurist Austin Walker called the game “an achievement” that was “remarkable” and “beautiful,” featuring puzzles that “capture a range of play that is largely abandoned by the digital form.” Fellow jurist Damon Reece shared in a blog post that the game is “seriously special to me” and that it gave him “a profound and powerful emotional reaction to being in a space that felt like home.”
But when it comes to IGF awards consideration, Walker and Reece were among those who said that even minimal use of AI tools overrode that deep and abiding respect for the work itself.
“We have our hands on the lever here,” Reece wrote. “This is pain that has to happen [emphasis in original] to try and steer our culture away from this. We need to choose to speak loudly and clearly on this, to prioritize human creativity and labour, to tell the culture and the world that this is unacceptable to us. To do otherwise is rank cowardice.”
This isn’t the first time AI usage has noticeably affected game award judging. Last year, the Indie Game Awards (which are completely separate from the IGF Awards) rescinded awards for Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 after the developers admitted that some in-game textures were made using AI tools (these were later patched out).
“The Indie Game Awards have a hard stance on the use of gen AI throughout the nomination process and during the ceremony itself,” they said at the time.
Since House House’s public disclosure, the anti-AI contingent of IGF judges has found plenty of support from disappointed Big Walk fans and industry observers. In the last few days, the game’s Steam page has been bombed with over 400 negative reviews, though Steam’s anti-review-bomb tools seem to be limiting the impact on the game’s overall “Very Positive” reception there.
But others feel House House’s relatively minimal use of AI here is being blown out of proportion. They say it’s important to differentiate between games that use LLMs as a last-resort technical fix, for instance, and others that lean heavily on AI to generate the bulk of their art, music, or the core of the game engine itself.
IGF judge Liz Ryerson wrote on social media that she didn’t find House House’s AI use to be personally disqualifying for the awards and that “the fact that many acted like there aren’t any levels to this and it’s all the same is bothersome to me.”
“To feel like someone gets punished a lot more for transparency about a smaller level of fuckup vs. just not even attempting to be honest or transparent at all is what bothers me,” she wrote.
Steam Hype staff writer and prolific Steam curator Dominic Tarason also pushed back against the idea that “House House need to be memory-holed and their work never spoken of again” as a “penalty for touching the Forbidden Device.” He said he considers Big Walk “very mildly compromised art” that is still “absolutely, unquestionably art and very human.”
“They spent years on that work of art,” Tarason added . “They asked a chatbot for two minutes how to fix a bug. That’s a ‘That’s lame, don’t do that again’ failing. … Some of you are acting like they’ve been convicted of high crimes against humanity, to be sealed away in the darkest oubliette until not even bones remain.”
But some have argued that using AI to fix a bug rather than hiring an expert to figure it out did make the game’s development at least a bit less human than it could have been. “House House aren’t laying off developers to replace them with Claude, and I’m sure they would be firmly against the mere thought of doing this, but we can also clearly see how their actions are part of the same problem,” AI researcher Mike Cook wrote on his blog .
Still, game developer, author, and professor Brendan Keogh wrote that he thinks “an extreme zero tolerance of any [generative AI] is ultimately counterproductive now. [There’s] a lot of anger at devs that feel deeply conflicted enough about their glorified Google search to disclose it, and [that is] encouraging those using it to actually steal labor to hide that use.”
As time goes on and AI tools are increasingly used in the building of major game engines , it may become increasingly difficult for anti-AI absolutists to avoid every game that has been touched by even a hint of LLM-generated code (if that use is even disclosed in the first place). articles.title_orig: The Rise and Rise of Alice Huang
articles.title_zh: The Rise and Rise of Alice Huang
articles.content_orig:
In 2019 Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Nvidia founder Jensen Huang, made $145 million from the sale of an online gaming group that three years earlier had annual revenues of just $36,000.
According to a securities filing , Ms Huang’s sale of her British Virgin Islands-based holding company, Osmanthus Vale Holdings Limited, came shortly after its revenues had soared 1,000 fold to $36 million in 2018. The transaction was also the catalyst for a dramatic career shift for Huang, also known by her Chinese name Huang Le, who by 2023 had risen to become managing director of a major data-center operator and Nvidia partner, Singapore-based Megaspeed.
The company that purchased Osmanthus from Huang was 7Road Holdings, a video game developer based in Shenzhen and listed on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.
In 2021, 7Road entered the cloud computing industry, just before the release of ChatGPT created a boom in such stocks. But when the Biden administration imposed export controls on China in October 2022, the company could no longer buy the most advanced AI chips from the likes of Nvidia.
7Road decided to spin off its Singapore subsidiary, which could buy America’s best AI chips. That subsidiary, 7Road International PTE, was sold to a BVI-registered company associated with Ms Huang and renamed Megaspeed.
Megaspeed went on to buy billions of dollars worth of servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips, and is the subject of U.S. and Singapore government investigations into whether it smuggled chips to China.
As of November 11, Nvidia continues to list Megaspeed as an official partner on its website.
The New York Times and Financial Times were the first to report, respectively, that U.S. officials suspected Ms Huang worked for China’s state security ministry and had an affair with Jensen Huang. China’s foreign ministry denied that Ms Huang worked for the MSS.
Jensen Huang told Bloomberg there was nothing improper about his relationship with Ms Huang.
The Nvidia founder subsequently admitted he had been unfaithful to his wife, but did not admit to an affair with Ms Huang.
President Donald Trump said that, in a phone call with Jensen Huang, the Nvidia founder told him he was unaware of any connections Ms Huang might have to China’s intelligence service. The scandal will hang over the president’s Asia trip next week to attend summits in the Philippines and China.
The 7Road deal was just one of many that would propel Ms Huang into the world of AI data centers.
She started her career as a news reporter for state television before moving into finance, according to her bio at an investment firm where she later worked. She eventually became the executive director of the firm, Shanghai Hexi Investment Fund, according to the Asset Management Association of China, a regulatory body.
Funds associated with Hexi invested alongside the Zhejiang Century Huatong Group, a maker of internet video games, as it entered the cloud computing business.
Between 2021 and 2022, Ms Huang served as a director of Shanghai Longjing Information Technology, according to corporate records accessed through WireScreen . The company was founded in December 2020 as a data-center focused subsidiary of Huatong. That same month, Huatong acquired a 10 percent stake in 7Road, securities filings show.
Seducing foreign executives is a common tactic used by China’s Ministry of State Security, especially on their visits to China, says Randal Phillips , a former CIA Beijing station chief. “The lion’s share of [MSS] resources were devoted to [compromising] private sector interests,” he adds.
WireScreen records show that Shanghai Longjing’s legal representative is Gu Jiong, who worked with Ms Huang at Shanghai Hexi Investment Fund, according to the fund’s website. Gu was also the legal representative of Hangzhou Shengfeng Network Technology, a Chinese video games company that Alice Huang sold to 7Road in 2019. Gu could not be reached for comment.
In 2023, the Shanghai municipal government announced that Shanghai Longjing would build a data center with 6,000 AI server racks at a larger complex where Tencent is a major tenant.
Tencent rents rack space from Shanghai Longjing that it fills with its own chips, according to people close to Tencent. When it is finished, the complex will provide 10 times as much computing power as the world’s largest supercomputer, according to Shanghai’s Songjiang district government .
A Tencent spokesperson said the company has never had a stake in, or operated, the complex.
It is not clear if Ms Huang held an operational role at Shanghai Longjing. She could not be reached for comment and the firm did not respond to a request for comment.
Huatong and 7Road did not respond to requests for comment.
Ms Huang’s involvement in several financing deals raises questions of whether she was a corporate fixer. Desmond Shum , whose ex-wife Duan Weihong held billions of dollars in shares of insurance company Ping An on behalf of the family of former Chinese premier Wen Jiabao, said Huang appeared to be a “white glove” — an investor whose name appears on documents on behalf of others.
In 2025, the China Securities Regulatory Commission fined Kang Wei, the founder of Shanghai Hexi, $375,000 for failing to make proper disclosures after he used complex investment vehicles to acquire an electronics company.
Osmanthus, Ms Huang’s video-game investment vehicle, had been incorporated in the British Virgin Islands less than two months before 7Road bought it, according to securities filings . Shanghai Hexi was the firm’s “ultimate holding company.”
Osmanthus’ biggest operating subsidiary was Hangzhou Shengfeng. According to a corporate filing , a Hexi-backed fund purchased Hangzhou Shengfeng from Century Huatong in 2017 for 500 million yuan (around $75 million). In 2019 the fund transferred Hangzhou Shengfeng to newly formed offshore entities, which were consolidated under Osmanthus, securities filings show.
That acquisition could explain the exponential jump in Osmanthus’ revenues, from $36,000 in 2016 to $36 million in 2018.
It is not clear how Ms Huang came to own 100 percent of Osmanthus.
“A woman whose documented career centered on corporate restructuring, leveraged acquisitions, and offshore holding companies suddenly emerged as the public face of [Megaspeed,] a multibillion-dollar AI infrastructure business,” Shum wrote on Substack.
Alice Huang served as Megaspeed’s managing director from March to November of 2023, according to corporate records. That November Megaspeed’s shares were transferred to another company, Swiftdata Pte, which had been incorporated just weeks earlier. By the end of 2024, Megaspeed’s assets had jumped to $3 billion, from just $33 million the year prior. The sole current director of Swiftdata is Tan Yong Pong, a Singaporean citizen, corporate records show.
Megaspeed said on Monday that there is “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities.” The company did not respond to a request for comment.
A spokesperson for the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, which enforces export controls, declined to comment when asked if it is considering taking any measures targeting Megaspeed.
Nvidia has long lobbied for weakening the export controls that prevent it from selling AI chips to China. President Trump loosened controls on Nvidia’s H200 chip last year.
Nvidia initially said Jensen Huang’s relationship with Ms Huang was “not unusual.” On Sunday, Nvidia’s board announced that it will open an inquiry into whether Jensen Huang was the target of a “foreign intelligence effort.” Its share price has dropped around 10 percent over the past five days.
The FBI is also looking into a matter related to Jensen Huang, Trump said at a press conference on Monday, without offering specifics.

articles.title_orig: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
articles.title_zh: American Airlines brings fresh food back to NY-Chicago first class for first time since 2019
articles.content_orig:
American Airlines said Wednesday it's bringing small, fresh "bites" to first class on flights between its hubs in New York and Chicago, the carrier's latest effort to win over higher-spending customers .
The changes start this month. Customers will be able to pick between two options, which include prosciutto and melon or apple cinnamon chia pudding for breakfast and a Thai noodle salad or mezze plate for lunch and dinner, American said Wednesday.
American last offered fresh food for first class on these routes in 2019, a spokeswoman said. Currently, customers in first class on these flights get a smaller, packaged snack. Airlines largely have limited food options for shorter flights, even in first class.
American has fallen behind Delta Air Lines and United Airlines in profits and investments in premium options. The airline has been working to step up those premium offerings in recent years with new cabins, lounges and plans for seatback screens on its narrow-body fleets.

articles.title_orig: Revenge of the China hawks: Jensen Huang’s enemies take a victory lap
articles.title_zh: Revenge of the China hawks: Jensen Huang’s enemies take a victory lap
articles.content_orig:
In the fall of 2025, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was riding high on the wave of the AI boom. He also landed at the center of an ideological war over chip exports that the $4 trillion company and its allies now think played a pivotal role in his undoing.
On one side were the China hawks inside the Trump administration â and circling outsiders â who worried Huangâs chips were helping fuel Chinaâs AI ambitions. On the other side were Huang, David Sacks, and other technologists that argued, often in their own self-interest, for spreading US tech around the globe to ensure American-backed AI became the world standard.
Huangâs long-held, pro-trade views were already unpopular with many of the think tankers, academics, national security staffers, and US government officials that make up a loosely held group of anti-China ideologues. But in a podcast interview with influential venture capitalists Bill Gurley and Brad Gerstner, Huang took things further, arguing the term âChina hawkâ is a badge of âshameâ and that those who wear it are not âpatriotic.â
The slight did not go unnoticed, drawing the ire of anti-technology voices like far-right podcast host Steve Bannon and other critics who had railed against Huangâs lobbying against strict China export controls.
âLetâs just say this â China hawks are patient and have long memories,â wrote Eric Sayers, a former Congressional defense staffer and current managing director of lobbyist Beacon Global Strategies, a firm that has done work on China policy, according to people familiar with the matter.
Sayers re-upped his year-old X post again on Nov. 2, days before Huang admitted to having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, on the back of weeks of media coverage digging into Megaspeed, an AI data center company based in Singapore that US government officials allege might be smuggling Nvidia chips into China. The implication was clear: Huangâs fate was not simply a result of the Nvidia CEOâs own personal failings or bad judgment. He had also made powerful enemies at the highest echelons of government that Nvidia now believes has all but stopped the companyâs ability to lobby for the export of chips to China, according to a person briefed on the matter.
Although thereâs no evidence to suggest they are connected to any leaks, among the most prominent of the China hawks are Sayersâ former colleague, Ivan Kanapathy, who serves as senior director for Asia at the National Security Council, and Tarun Chhabra, who served as deputy assistant to the president and coordinator for technology and national security on the National Security Council, and Landon Heid, an NSC staffer who nearly became assistant secretary of commerce for export administration at the Bureau of Industry and Security.
Chhabra now works for Anthropic, another vocal critic of export controls, with CEO Dario Amodei comparing chip sales to China to selling nuclear weapons to North Korea. Anthropic has also accused Chinese AI companies of stealing its intellectual property in order to train open weight AI models.
Spokespeople for Nvidia, the White House, Commerce Department, State Department, NSC, Marco Rubio, and Beacon Global didnât immediately respond to requests for comment.
Itâs unclear who was responsible for leaking national security documents that were used to discredit Huang. And whether the Nvidia CEO was the target of an espionage plot, or if there was any wrongdoing on his or Nvidiaâs part, will be determined by investigators in the months ahead. But the damage has already shaved about $280 billion off the market value of the $4.2 trillion company. Huangâs now facing a board probe, shareholder lawsuits, Congressional questioning, and the near-certain prospect of details leaking out in drips and drabs.
Several people familiar with their China policy agenda say the group of hawks wield considerable power and influence in DC, and the elimination of Huang from the other side of the debate will make the upcoming fight over export controls being added to the National Defense Authorization Act significantly easier.
Huang obviously walked into a scandal, but the US government bears some responsibility for clearing up whether or not itâs investigating the founder of the countryâs most successful company, potentially harming a company with massive strategic value and shaving off billions of dollars of a stock thatâs in most peopleâs investment accounts.
Nvidiaâs success and failure has direct and indirect impacts on almost everybody in the US, and many around the world. We should get a full accounting of the impacts of an extrajudicial action against a US citizen by the government with enormous economic implications, positive and negative. Either something is classified or itâs not. Now that itâs been leaked, the rest of the information should be made public.
From James Czerniawski, head of emerging technology policy at the Consumer Choice Center. âThe government shouldnât be able to weaponize a surveillance file against an American and their business. It should concern every American whenever intelligence is selectively surfaced and leveraged to advance certain policies, whether that means tighter chip export controls or building support for reauthorizing a deeply flawed surveillance program. When the government wields this kind of power, it isnât just disrupting an individualâs life; it can put a target on an American company and create economic uncertainty in the marketplace. That kind of power demands real limitations and accountability. Protecting our national security is important, but giving the government carte blanche to use its surveillance capabilities is a recipe for disaster that will ultimately leave everyone worse off.â

articles.title_orig: Heating Costs Will Rise 7% on Average This Winter
articles.title_zh: Heating Costs Will Rise 7% on Average This Winter
articles.content_orig:
Nearly 5m households relying on heating oil could see 70% increases, as advocates call on Congress to provide relief
Americans are likely to face higher heating bills this winter amid a growing affordability crisis, with costs projected to climb more than 7% nationwide and some households facing increases of up to 70%, according to a new report.
The National Energy Assistance Directors Association (Neada), which represents state officials seeking federal funding, warns that disruptions stemming from the war with Iran are pushing heating costs higher as millions of families already struggle to pay utility bills.
Households relying on heating oil, particularly in the north-east and Alaska , face the biggest increases. Nearly 5m households use the fuel, with seasonal costs potentially jumping 70%, to approximately $2,977.
The north-east is expected to see average heating bills rise 16.9%, or $221, from $1,311 last winter to $1,532 this winter. The region has some of the nation’s highest electricity prices and the greatest concentration of heating oil customers.
“For higher-income households, these increases may be an inconvenience. For low- and middle-income families, they can be devastating,” said Mark Wolfe, executive director of Neada, in a statement.
“Families are already struggling with rising costs for food, housing and other necessities. Adding hundreds or even thousands of dollars to their winter heating bills will push many of them further into debt.”
Global fuel supply disruptions are adding pressure. Supplies have tightened as refineries in the Middle East and Russia shut down or cut production amid the US-Israel war with Iran and Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine.
Wolfe wrote last month about how the Iran war is deepening the US’s energy crisis, describing heating oil as “the canary in the coalmine” for the broader affordability crisis.
“The situation in the strait of Hormuz remains highly volatile, and continued uncertainty about global oil supplies makes it difficult to predict where prices will go,” Wolfe said. “For planning purposes, we believe it is prudent to assume that heating oil prices will remain elevated throughout the winter heating season.”
The projected increases come as roughly one in six US households are behind on utility payments, collectively owing about $23bn, Neada reported.
Other households are expected to pay more as well. Electric heating costs could increase about 6%, to $1,215, while propane bills are projected to rise roughly 5%, to an average of $1,350.
The warning follows a record-hot summer that saw widespread financial hardship and electricity shutoffs. In July, the hottest month ever recorded in the US, utilities disconnected power to 173,598 households across 10 states despite dangerous temperatures.
With winter bills expected to climb, Neada is urging Congress to provide relief.
“Energy is not a luxury. Families need to be able to heat their homes without worrying about whether they can afford food, medicine or rent,” Wolfe said. “Congress has an opportunity to provide immediate relief before these higher winter bills arrive.”

articles.title_orig: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
articles.title_zh: Toyota’s Scion is back, starting with an American-made, 25-mph kei truck
articles.content_orig:
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.﻿
Toyota is reviving the Scion badge as an experimental mobility incubator—starting with an Indiana-built, 25-mph kei truck engineered for American fleets.﻿
Toyota is dusting off the Scion badge for a radically different mission. Rather than targeting youth-market hatchbacks, “Scion by Toyota” is being positioned as an experimental mobility incubator — and its first vehicle is an authentic Japanese-style kei truck built in Indiana.
Kei vehicles, which are built to satisfy Japan’s light vehicle regulations, are enjoying surging popularity around the world, including here in the US. More than 30,000 used kei trucks have been imported into the US since 2020, with roughly 7,500 units entering the country each year. Even President Trump is a fan , telling reporters last year that he authorized the Department of Transportation to approve their production.
Toyota looks to be the first to test the American market’s appetite for the tiny trucks. The choice to use the Scion brand, which was discontinued in 2016 , would seem to indicate that the automaker is hoping to appeal to younger car buyers. But more than that, Toyota says it sees Scion as a testing ground for utility, outdoor adventure, and customization that wouldn’t typically fit in any of its other models.
When it lands in the second half of 2027, Scion’s KEI-01 sports a 660cc three-cylinder gas engine paired with a continuously variable transmission. It won’t win any drag races, but it should delivery enough power for stop-and-go driving while using a minimum amount of fuel.
It’s true super power comes from its diminutive dimensions. At roughly 11 feet long and under 5 feet wide, the KEI-01 is about half the footprint of a full-size pickup. It can easily thread through cramped alleys, narrow barn aisles, garden gates, or busy campus pathways where standard trucks can’t fit.
The truck features an on-demand 4WD system with a push-button locking mode. If you’re cutting across muddy farm turf, gravel work paths, or wet slush, power splits to all four wheels to keep the truck from spinning out or getting stuck.
Inside, the vehicle looks pretty cheap, with lots of black plastic and a noticeable absence of any premium materials. That will hopefully help keep the price nice and low — though Toyota hasn’t disclosed any trim options yet. Japanese imports typically range from $6,000 to $12,000.
Because it is certified under federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) rules — also used for golf carts and golf cart-adjacent vehicles — its top speed is strictly capped at 25 mph. The truck bed features three sides that fold completely flat, removing the need to lean over high-metal sides to drop in cargo. The KEI-01 can hold up to 600 pounds of soil, tools, or gear, and can easily tow small utility trailers or mowers.
Unlike an open utility cart or ATV, this tiny truck has a fully sealed cabin equipped with both heating and air conditioning. The extended roofline gives drivers extra headroom, reclining seats, and interior storage behind the seats to keep tools dry and secure. True to classic Japanese utility imports, the steering wheel is on the right side of the cab. Beyond the cool factor, curbside delivery and stepping directly onto sidewalks or worksite shoulders is quicker and safer.
To make the KEI-01 to conform to the rules and regs of auto manufacturing in the US, Toyota is investing $34 million into its Princeton, Indiana manufacturing plant to stand up local assembly and add roughly 50 jobs. Production kicks off in the second half of 2027, but everyday drivers won’t be able to buy one off the lot immediately.
Scion by Toyota is launching the mini-truck strictly as a fleet-focused pilot program targeting corporate campuses, farms, municipalities, and local delivery operators, distributed through a specialized group of existing Toyota dealerships. While Toyota notes it may consider opening up sales to consumer retail down the road if demand justifies it, the initial rollout is very much treated as an experiment to evaluate real-world US utility.
The KEI-01 was joined by two adventure-themed concepts that show Scion’s new focus extends far beyond budget hatchbacks. The SxS Concept packs a 300-plus-horsepower hybrid turbo setup for high-speed off-roading, while the modular BKE Concept explores compact personal mobility. Together, they signal that Scion’s second act is aimed squarely at niche utility and experimental recreation.

articles.title_orig: Apple is shuttering its 28-year-old online community forum
articles.title_zh: Apple is shuttering its 28-year-old online community forum
articles.content_orig:
Apple’s online community forum will close on November 20.
On Tuesday night, Apple posted a message to the Apple Support Community announcing the forum’s closure:
The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.
You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site .
We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.
For 28 years, the forum has provided Apple users with a way to get quick technical advice about their products. That advice usually came from fellow users, though Apple employees occasionally chimed in. As with any community forum, the helpfulness and accuracy of the advice varied.
Apple reportedly told MacRumors that it is shutting down the forum after evaluating its support strategy and customer needs.
The Apple Support Community dates to 1998, when the online forum was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Two years later, Apple renamed the community forum to Apple Discussions. In 2011 , Apple revamped the forum, adding dedicated communities for specific devices and the ability to track responses to posted questions, while renaming it Apple Support Communities. By 2022, the forum was called Apple Support Community, as MacRumors noted this week.
Based on yesterday’s announcement, it seems Apple now prefers that its customers rely on official Apple employees for technical support. The forum may also have become less popular as rival forums grow, including Reddit and the technical support communities on the MacRumors and AppleInsider forums.

Alison Quinn, president of Dinova, tells Fox News Digital how participating restaurants are showing appreciation for America's military community through complimentary menu items and promotional offers, including incentives for future visits.
Veterans and active-duty military members can find free food and other promotions at restaurants across the country on Veterans Day, Nov. 11. Some offers also give customers a reason to return for another deal later.
About 30 restaurant brands are included in Dinova's 2026 Veterans Day Dining Guide , according to Alison Quinn, the company's Florida-based president.
The guide is in its fifth year and includes national and regional chains like Bonefish Grill, Carrabba's Italian Grill, Hooters, Outback Steakhouse and Red Lobster.

U.S. stock futures traded mixed overnight late Monday after markets recovered following a steep AI selloff last week.
Nvidia Corp. (NVDA) was in focus at the start of the week after the chipmaker's board said it would be launching an independent investigation into CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.
Markets will now be watching for October’s consumer price index and producer price index data this week for cues on the health of the U.S. economy.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
As of 11:06 p.m. EST, Dow futures gained 0.33%, while the S&P 500 futures were up 0.01% and Nasdaq-100 futures declined 0.37%.
On Monday, the three U.S. benchmark indexes rallied after a massive selloff last week. The Dow Jones Industrial Average added more than 1,100 points to close 2.15% higher. The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.35% and 2.74%, respectively.
On Monday, markets rallied after a volatile week for stocks, especially artificial intelligence and technology names, which plunged last week as traders grew increasingly concerned about a slowdown in data center buildouts after Democrats posted victories in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
Meanwhile, contentious reports around Nvidia led to a slump in the company’s shares, which closed more than 4% lower on Monday, after CEO Jensen Huang admitted over the weekend to having an affair with a woman who is suspected of being a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. While the company’s board of directors launched an independent internal investigation, it also expressed confidence in the CEO. A fresh investor lawsuit has been filed against Nvidia as well on Monday.
The rest of the AI trade recovered on Monday, posting gains. The iShares Semiconductor ETF (SOXX) jumped 7.49% at close, while the VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) gained 5%.
Funstrat’s Tom Lee said in an interview with CNBC on Monday that there seemed to be encouraging news for the markets.
Advertisement | Remove ads.
“The first is we had a flurry of bad news over the weekend, one involving Nvidia and some about Texas going after Elon Musk's companies. And yet the markets are at those stocks are rallying today. I think that's a good sign that markets are rallying on bad news,” he said.
“But the second is the VIX, the VIX term structure, which is the four-month VIX versus the one-month, inverted last week. It's now normalized today. That's usually a sign of a bottom. So I think that this is more proof that last week was the low,” Lee added.
Ross Gerber, co-founder and CEO at Gerber Kawasaki, also expressed confidence in the markets. In a post on X, Gerber said, “Stocks are way too cheap and this moment won't last long.  Economy is strong. Earnings are strong. Consumer is still strong. Higher rates not denting infrastructure investment. Of course no war all TACO.  Oil prices down. Inflation dropping now. Trump lost the people so some sanity will return to our government. Market correction in. Was very busy at the end of last week.”

On the geopolitical front, a conclusion on the U.S.-Iran war is yet to arrive, although U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with CNBC over the weekend that he is “highly unlikely” to restart a full-fledged war with Iran if there is progress made in the talks on Tehran’s nuclear program and the reopening of the critical Strait of Hormuz.
Trump also met with Qatar's prime minister, Sheik Mohammed bin Abdulrahman, at the White House on Monday in a closed-door meeting.
In a post on Truth Social, Trump said that he had an “excellent conversation” with the Prime Minister of Qatar, which included discussions about Iran. “Should there be any change with respect to developments in the Middle East, the United States of America is “locked and loaded” and ready to go. We are seeing positive momentum toward an end to this Conflict, and will ensure that America’s interests are at all times protected. At the conclusion of this Military Engagement, the American People, and the World, will be far safer and more secure,” he added.

articles.title_orig: Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.title_zh: Gibran Rakabuming Raka: Indonesia's vice president resigns amid signs ruling alliance is fraying
articles.content_orig:
Indonesia's Vice-President Gibran Rakabuming Raka has submitted his resignation, an aide has told the BBC, in a move which could further strain the political alliance that helped propel President Prabowo Subianto to power.
It comes after Indonesia's Supreme Court ruled that a high-school document used during Gibran's 2024 election campaign was invalid.
The ruling prompted more than 100 lawmakers to support a parliamentary initiative that could have paved the way for proceedings to impeach Gibran.
The aide, Budi Arie, said Gibran's resignation letter was submitted directly to Prabowo on Wednesday. It remains unclear if it has been accepted.
Gibran has long faced controversy over whether his high school qualifications met legal requirements to run for office.
Having studied in Singapore and Australia, he had used an Indonesian equivalence certificate to demonstrate his educational credentials.
Indonesian law requires vice-presidents to have completed senior secondary school or its equivalent, but the Supreme Court found no evidence to prove Gibran had graduated.
"No evidence was found to show Gibran had a foreign diploma or certificate that could serve as the basis for equivalency with a senior high school or equivalent qualification," it said.
It also considered a Constitutional Court ruling from earlier in October which came to the same conclusion.
Gibran previously argued that undertaking university education was sufficient proof that he had completed senior high school.
On Tuesday, he asked for the chance to challenge the ruling and be given the opportunity to prove the legitimacy of his education credentials, State Secretary Prasetyo Hadi said.
Gibran's ascension to Prabowo's ticket in the 2024 election was part of an alliance formed between his father, outgoing president Joko Widodo - known as Jokowi - and Prabowo, his erstwhile bitter rival.
Gibran was 36 at the time, and only became eligible for candidacy after a controversial ruling by the Constitutional Court, which exempted him from the minimum age requirement of 40.
His resignation comes as tensions between Jokowi and Prabowo appear to have flared.
Since taking the presidency, Prabowo has shown little interest in pushing ahead with Jokowi's legacy project: the construction of Nusantara, a new capital. Instead, he has focused much of the state's resources on his own flagship programme to provide free school meals across the country.
In a series of personnel reshuffles over the past year, Prabowo has also shifted many Jokowi loyalists into new roles, including long-serving finance minister Sri Mulyani Indrawati.
Last week, authorities arrested presidential chief of staff Listyo Sigit Prabowo - no relation - on suspicions of wiretapping the president.
Prabowo sacked Listyo a day later, in what many pointed to as a sign of a crumbling alliance: Listyo, who formerly served as the national police chief, is widely considered a long-time ally of Jokowi.
Within the government, allegiances seem to be shifting. On Monday, three members of Prabowo's cabinet collectively resigned from the party led by Kaesang Pangarep, Jokowi's youngest son, citing their desire to focus on their duties in Prabowo's administration.
All this is unfolding at a particularly turbulent period in Prabowo's presidency. The  free school meals programme is struggling for funding, parts of Indonesia have recently battled the country's worst wildfires in a decade, and the national stock market faces crisis amid allegations of widespread market manipulation.
On Tuesday, students across the country staged demonstrations to protest against the government's handling of a range of issues, including the environmental crisis and corruption.

articles.title_orig: China select board deals with complicated issues
articles.title_zh: China select board deals with complicated issues
articles.content_orig:
China select board members had several complicated issues on their Nov. 2 agenda, not all ripe for decision. They decided three:
— Board members unanimously approved a new, less comprehensive proposal from Raegan LaRochelle to assist with developing China’s revised Tax Increment Financing (TIF) plan (see the Oct. 22 issue of The Town Line, p. 3 ). LaRochelle will receive $3,200 for about three weeks spent educating the select board and the public and working with them and Town Manager Rebecca Hapgood to identify town projects eligible for TIF funding. Her fee will come from the TIF account. — After discussion of the town’s partly-outdated Telecommunications Ordinance, board members unanimously accepted Harmoni Towers’ bond in the amount of $68,637.75. The bond is intended to cover the cost of removal when the tower the company has approval to build on Parmenter Hill becomes obsolete (see the Oct. 29 issue of The Town Line, p. 2 ). The bond amount did not have the professional engineer’s endorsement that the ordinance requires. Codes Officer Nicholas French said confirming removal cost estimates is “not what professional engineers do.” — By yet another unanimous vote, board members changed China’s HRA (Health Reimbursement Account) from the current administrator to Consumer Health Solutions, saving $470 and, Hapgood hopes, getting as good or better service.
The HRA is related to the town employees’ health insurance plan, topic of a quarter-hour discussion and no decision. The Maine Municipal Employees Health Trust currently offers five plans; China is enrolled in the middle one, in terms of employee costs and benefits. The town would save money by switching to a less generous plan.
Hapgood said with the HRA covering employees’ costs, like deductibles and co-pays, last year was the first year the town didn’t “make employees whole.”
She invited select board members to send her questions to be answered at the Nov. 16 board meeting. With open enrollment starting Nov. 15, she expects a decision on Nov. 16.
Another issue involving money and potential complications is dispatching emergency services. Currently, China uses the Kennebec Sheriff’s Office (KSO), which in turn uses the state system. This system, Select Board Chairman Brent Chesley said he learned at a meeting the previous week, is outdated, and the state won’t spend money to update it.
Therefore, KSO intends to switch to the City of Augusta’s dispatching service, at a higher cost.
Chesley was indignant about several aspects of the planned new system. Each town’s charge is based on a 1987 formula, 75 percent on population and 25 percent on call volume, which he said is contrary to state statute.
The formula also hurts China and Chelsea, two Kennebec County towns that contract for KSO patrols, Chesley said. Every time a KSO deputy calls in to check a license plate, China gets billed for a call.
Chesley was more indignant because he had learned that towns with their own dispatching service don’t pay the county anything. He said he asked at the meeting if there is a county service China doesn’t use, can the town be exempted from paying for it?
A final insult, he said, was when county officials proposed starting the new service – and billing for it – on April 1, instead of waiting for the towns’ new fiscal years to begin July 1.
The dispatch bill will be separate from the annual county tax bill, he said.
Also needing decision soon is whether to renew the contract for disposal of bulky waste and construction debris or to seek a new company. The current contract with Waste Management ends Dec. 31. Hapgood said Transfer Station Manager Thomas Maraggio is seeking prices from several services.
Board members heard of, but did not discuss, one more potential expense increase, for Delta Ambulance. The towns of Fairfield and Benton have notified Delta that they intend to stop using its service in February 2027. Delta officials will have to find some way to continue to pay bills without those two towns.
As the meeting ended, Hapgood reminded those present that all town departments will be closed Wednesday, Nov. 11, for the Veterans’ Day holiday; and Thursday and Friday, Nov. 26 and 27, for the Thanksgiving holiday.
The Nov. 16 select board meeting is scheduled for 6 p.m. in the town office meeting room.

SpaceX is counting down to make history with the launch of its Starship Flight 15 mission on Friday, Nov. 13 , with liftoff scheduled for 5:45 p.m. EDT (2245 GMT) at Starbase, Texas. Starship Flight 15 will attempt to land both Starship Ship and Super Heavy Booster. It will be the first-ever full recovery of an orbital rocket and spacecraft, if successful.
Follow our Starship Flight 15 coverage here as SpaceX completes its final prelaunch work for the launch, which will also deliver 26 new Starlink V3 satellites into orbit.

Happy Wednesday, Space Fans. We are now T-2 days away from SpaceX's planned launch of its Starship Flight 15 test mission, so I wanted to take a moment to give you a run down on what to expect.
Today, you can read my full guide to SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch here , which goes over what time and where to watch the launch online. Liftoff is on track for Friday, Nov. 13, at 4:45 p.m. CST, which is 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT). But it ALSO (and this is new) includes what time to tune in a day later for the planned Starship upper stage (Ship) landing and catch by the metal "Chopstick" arms of its landing pad at SpaceX's Starbase facility in South Teas.
If you're wondering how the rocket's assembly is going, our Spaceflight Editor Mike Wall has this update on the Starship Flight 15 Super Heavy booster going through final catch tests yesterday. Flight 15 will mark the first time SpaceX will attempt to land and catch both the Super Heavy booster (which it has done several times) and the Ship from orbit.
If successful, it will be the first full recovery of an entire orbital rocket from space.
Hello, Space Fans, and welcome to our coverage of SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 test flight , the first ever to attempt twin landings of the Starship Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage.
SpaceX has officially set the launch date for Flight 15 for Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EDT (2145 GMT) . That puts launch just about 3 days away and Space.com will provide live coverage of the potentially historic flight, the first full recovery of an orbital rocket.
Space.com Spaceflight Writer Josh Dinner will be reporting live from near SpaceX's Starbase , Texas site for the launch, with myself (Tariq Malik), Spaceflight and Tech Editor Mike Wall and other team members tracking the flight remotely for you here. SpaceX has already test-fired the engines on its Starship Flight 15 vehicles.
Today, SpaceX moved Super Heavy Booster 22 , the first stage for Flight 15, to the launch pad for vehicle stacking. Here are some photos of that move:
Super Heavy moved to the launch pad at Starbase. Booster 22 is the first Super Heavy V3 booster planned to return to the launch site for catch and was used for final catch testing upon arrival, including a suspended squeeze test at catch height https://t.co/iYTX1e6DEH November 10, 2026

articles.title_orig: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
articles.title_zh: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
articles.content_orig:
Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain
            the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in
            Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles
            and JavaScript.
The scarcity of terrestrial rocks older than 3.9 billion years (Gyr) has hindered our understanding of Earth’s early evolution, fuelling persistent debates on how and when the first continental crust formed and plate tectonics started. At present, the only unequivocally documented >3.9-Gyr-old rocks are from the Acasta Gneiss Complex, Canada 1 , 2 , 3 . Here we report a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, North China Craton, in which primary magmatic zircon records elevated δ 18 O values (average +6.77 ± 0.23‰) and positive ε Hf ( t ) values (weighted mean +1.45 ± 0.27). This suggests a low-temperature altered basaltic source that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean. In contrast to the low-pressure origin inferred for the roughly 4.0-Gyr-old Idiwhaa unit in Acasta 2 , the 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss reported here exhibits geochemical signatures attributed to a high-pressure origin 4 . Thermodynamic and trace element modelling demonstrate that its parental magma formed by means of low-degree (8–16%) melting of basaltic crust at >1.6 GPa and 740–820 °C, suggesting rapid burial of (near-)surface-altered oceanic crust to mantle depths along a cool thermal gradient. We propose that this rapid burial was most likely achieved through a transient subduction event.

articles.title_orig: CoreWeave Shares Soar After AI Computing Firm Eases Debt Fears
articles.title_zh: CoreWeave Shares Soar After AI Computing Firm Eases Debt Fears
articles.content_orig:
CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC on Wednesday that he has canceled his 10b5 stock sale plan after the company reported strong revenue growth and beat Q3 expectations .
"Until there is a material change in in, in our equity pricing, my 10b5 has been sidelined," he told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street."
He said any further selling would be "just normal tax stuff."
Under Intrator's 10b5-1 plan announced in November 2025, the CEO has sold 8.26 million shares at an average price of $96.14 per share for a total of $794.2 million.
Intrator and his co-founders have faced criticism for their stock sales as the company's stock has struggled, with shares down 18% so far in 2026 despite a 20% post-earnings rally on Wednesday.
The company has faced further pressure from the sell-off in the aftermath of last week's sweeping electoral victory for Democrats, but Intrator told investors on the earnings call that the company isn't worried about the political changes on the horizon.
"We do not anticipate any impact from the seismic regulatory shift that's occurred," Intrator said on his company's earnings call late Tuesday, in response to a question about new pressures after the election. "We believe that what has occurred is a statement around how you build. We want to build responsibly."
Intrator's comments came after CoreWeave reported 168% year-over-year revenue growth, beating estimates, and lifted its forecast for 2026. The stock rallied in extended trading, as the report offered some relief to investors, who have pushed the shares down about 27% over the past month.
Rising interest rates and an unfavorable political environment have fueled concerns that the artificial intelligence boom is poised to cool and that companies like CoreWeave will struggle to raise capital.
In the Nov. 3 midterm elections, voters sided in favor of greater restrictions on data centers in 40 out of 41 ballot measures in 10 states, according to Ballotpedia . Democrats won control of both houses of Congress and were victorious in governors' races in critical AI infrastructure states like Texas, Ohio and Georgia. In each state, the winning candidate favors some restrictions on new data centers.
J.P. Morgan Asset Management wrote in a report after the election that data center projects from 2028 onward are "most exposed," and "face greater uncertainty around permitting, power availability and financing."
But CoreWeave says it's not slowing down. The company said it still anticipates 1.85 gigawatts in active power by the end of 2026, and it's now targeting $37 billion to $39 billion in full-year capital expenditures,  implying 155% growth at the middle of the range. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha were looking for $37.69 billion.
"We are very comfortable with our pipeline," Intrator said, adding that the message from voters isn't a deterrent because the company is always conscious about "being good neighbors."
"We think that that is an opportunity for us to continue to scale our business within the new political reality that exists," Intrator said.
—CNBC's Nick Wells contributed to this article.

articles.title_orig: China seeks 'tangible progress' in ties with US as top diplomat Wang speaks to Rubio ahead of APEC summit
articles.title_zh: China seeks 'tangible progress' in ties with US as top diplomat Wang speaks to Rubio ahead of APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi spoke by telephone Wednesday with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, emphasizing Beijing's desire to achieve "tangible progress" in relations ahead of upcoming multilateral leader gatherings.
"China is ready to strengthen communication and cooperation with the US side, properly handle differences and sensitive issues," Wang told Rubio, according to China's Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning.
Beijing and Washington support each other in the "successful hosting" of the APEC Summit and the G20 Leaders’ Summit, and "work for tangible progress in building a constructive China-US relationship of strategic stability," said Wang.
Wang affirmed that China's broader policy toward Washington remains "stable and consistent" as both powers prepare for senior diplomatic engagements.
Chins said the call was "positive and constructive."
"Stable momentum of China-US ties did not come easily and is the two major countries' rational choice based on respective and common interests," said Wang, according to a statement by the Foreign Ministry.
The call comes as Chinese President Xi Jinping prepares to host regional heads of state for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting from Nov. 18 - 19 in China. The summit will gather representatives from 21 member economies, including US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, amid reports of a potential trilateral meeting involving Putin in Shenzhen.
Xi and Trump, during their two summits this year in Beijing and Washington, have agreed to build a "constructive relationship of strategic stability based on respect, fairness and reciprocity," according to China.
The US State Department had not released a readout of the call as of 10.50 am Washington time (1550GMT).

articles.title_orig: US postpones ‘million-dollar’ China ship tax until January
articles.title_zh: US postpones ‘million-dollar’ China ship tax until January
articles.content_orig:
The United States has extended the suspension of port fees targeting China-linked shipping for another two months, keeping the measures on hold through January 9, 2027, according to a notice published Tuesday in the Federal Register.
The decision gives Washington and Beijing additional time to negotiate over Chinese policies affecting the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding industries.
The Office of the United States Trade Representative said the extension took effect November 9 and runs through 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time on January 9. It follows a one-year suspension that began November 10, 2025, under a trade agreement announced by President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.
The pause also continues to cover additional duties on Chinese ship-to-shore cranes and other cargo-handling equipment specified in the agency’s earlier action.
China also extended its suspension of reciprocal port fees on U.S.-linked vessels until January 10.
USTR said the circumstances supporting the original suspension remain in place and that further discussions with China are needed.
The U.S. fees could amount to millions of dollars for a single vessel’s visit. A 50,000-net ton ship, for example, would owe $2.5 million in charges.
The measures arose from the U.S. investigation under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 into China’s targeting of the maritime, logistics and shipbuilding sectors for dominance. The suspended fee categories include charges affecting Chinese-owned or operated vessels, Chinese-built vessels and foreign-built vehicle carriers.
In comments to USTR, supporters of the pause argued that it would avoid higher shipping costs, prevent commercial disruptions and provide time for negotiations. Some sought permanent suspension of certain fees, warning that their return could disrupt trade and harm U.S. exports.
Opponents argued that the fees are needed to encourage investment in American shipbuilding and related industries, including container manufacturing. Some commenters also urged USTR to treat cargo-equipment tariffs separately from maritime service fees and end the suspension of those tariffs.
USTR said the United States will use the additional negotiating period to pursue its concerns with China while continuing efforts to expand domestic commercial shipbuilding capacity, develop the workforce and cooperate with allies.
Why it matters: The reciprocal pause averts additional shipping costs and potential disruptions affecting not only U.S. and Chinese carriers but also businesses worldwide that rely on Chinese-built vessels. It gives importers, exporters and shipowners temporary relief while trade negotiations continue.

Tabletop provides customizable, collaborative spaces for all your personal planning needs.﻿
Google has cooked up a new experimental AI tool called Tabletop that generates customized collaborative hubs to help you coordinate with family, and friends. The Tabletop platform shares some visual similarities with workplace management apps like Asana and Monday, but with a built-in AI feature that allows you to vibecode personalized interactive tools by describing them, such as savings trackers, chore charts, event plans, and more.
“Just add in your links, files and ideas, then prompt @tabletop — or pick a starter template — to generate custom interactive trip itineraries, dinner polls, expense splitters and tournament brackets,” Google Labs design and engineering lead Roman Nurik said in the blog post. “Once your space is ready, drop the invite link in your group chat to let everyone jump in and use it at the same time like a Google Doc.”
Access to the Tabletop beta is rolling out via a waitlist , and currently limited to people over the age of 18 in the US. Some of the example use cases that Nurik provides in his video above would clearly require giving kids or teens access to Tabletop, however, and using this for personal family planning looks like a compelling alternative to stuffy workplace software, so that age requirement might only be in place while Tabletop is in public testing.

Hello, this is Leonie Kidd with today's edition of Morning Squawk.
CoreWeave is providing the tailwind for futures today, helping lift neocloud stocks, while a rebound for Nvidia is also supporting the chip space.
But is it enough to dull the lingering doubts around the AI trade?
CoreWeave shares are surging in premarket trading, up over 16% overnight, after the neocloud group posted a 168% spike in third-quarter revenue.
The group also lifted its 2026 guidance , driving other neocloud stocks higher.
But bear in mind that shares are down 65% from their May highs, losing over 40% of their value in the last month alone.
Nvidia shares are extending gains in premarket trading, up just over 3%.
The move is also supporting gains for Broadcom , AMD , Intel and Nebius .
Here are the key developments:
CNBC's Seema Mody spoke to sources within Nvidia who said Huang walked into the group's Santa Clara, California, headquarters on Monday to hold his regular meeting with top-level executives.
To go inside that meeting, read the full piece here on CNBC.com.
Anthropic is offering 825 million shares at a price range of $70-78 per share.
Sources close to the deal told CNBC the AI titan is planning to price on November 18 and trade on November 19.
CNBC's Morning Squawk recaps the biggest stories investors should know before the stock market opens, every weekday morning.
Subscribe here to get access today .
The House of Representatives has effectively voted down an attempt to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
The House, by a 211-204 margin, approved a measure that will refer the impeachment resolution to a committee, leaving little time for it to be acted on before Democrats take over in January.
Tokenization: The next evolution of the stock market
The U.S. equity market has repeatedly changed its underlying mechanics while the asset itself — a share of stock — has remained largely the same.
Trading moved from floors and phone calls to electronic venues. Settlement cycles compressed. Commissions fell to zero. Fractional shares and online brokerages expanded retail participation.
The next major change may already be underway.
