articles.title_orig: The Kraft Group wants to build a $16 billion data center campus in a small Central Mass. town
articles.title_zh: The Kraft Group wants to build a $16 billion data center campus in a small Central Mass. town
articles.content_orig:
New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft’s company is stepping into a political minefield, proposing to build one of the largest data centers in the country in the Central Massachusetts town of Sutton, just as opposition to the facilities is intensifying.
In this area, known for its farmland and home to about 9,700 residents, the Kraft Group would build a massive, $16 billion data center campus. The project would include 10 buildings, erected on land owned by the Krafts’ Unified Packaging box business about 10 miles south of Worcester. It would push Massachusetts into the world of big data centers, as the fourth-biggest facility in the United States, according to the research firm Cleanview.
The proposal must be approved by multiple town committees before moving ahead, and it puts Kraft once again at the center of political controversy , this time as data centers have become political poison across the country . Voters last week from Maine to California approved 44 referendums to block or slow data center construction. Last month, the Western Massachusetts community of Westfield moved to block a large data center proposed there.
The Sutton Select Board met Tuesday night to hear about the project amid a packed hearing room. Chair Jonathan Anderson said the board would not immediately vote on the matter and planned to hold multiple public forums to discuss the proposal with the community.
“This is not a project that’s a done deal,” he said. “It’s far from it. This is the very, very beginning of the process.”
The board allowed only about 15 minutes of public comments at the start of the meeting and all six speakers said they opposed the project. “I would like to see this process stopped tonight,” Sutton resident Sarah Osterman Stone said.
The crowd remained rowdy after the public comments, shouting as the board tried to move on with its business. “Kill it now,” one person shouted. “Just end the process,” another added.
The Sutton proposal would dwarf the Westfield project. When completed in 2033, the Kraft data center would draw 900 megawatts of electricity, enough to power a sizable city. Three larger data centers are already in operation; many larger projects are in the planning or construction stages, including Meta’s 6,500 megawatt data center in Louisiana.
Given the fierce opposition to data center construction and comments at Tuesday’s meeting, the Kraft Group is likely to face strong local opposition. Residents have also been stirring in comments on social media.
“There’s been a pretty quick response from the community expressing concerns,” said state Representative Joe McKenna, who represents the area. The main issues are that the project could drive up electricity rates, consume too much water, and generate noise, he said. “They’re concerns that I share, but I’m also not willing to say ‘No’ just based on a fear of an unknown, or fear of an uncertainty,” McKenna added.
Sutton’s town manager, Austin J. Cyganiewicz, confirmed the $16 billion proposal from the Kraft Group and Unified Global Packaging Group in a letter sent Monday to the town’s Select Board.
The Kraft Group did not return a request for comment Tuesday.
The Krafts clashed last summer with Foxborough town officials over $8 million in security costs for the World Cup. And in September, Robert Kraft drew wide criticism for barring rap artist Macklemore from performing at Gillette Stadium over his remarks in support of Palestinians.
As for the move into data centers, Massachusetts has so far not been an appealing destination for the large, energy-hungry facilities powering the AI boom — Sutton would be the first. That’s because the state has among the highest electricity rates in the country, not to mention high land prices and construction costs, IDC analyst Matt Eastwood said.
But as the AI boom moves from early development to broader usage, every part of the country will need local, large data centers, according to Eastwood.
If approved, the first two buildings at the Sutton site, off Boston and Providence roads, would open in 2029, and two more facilities would come online each year through 2033, for a total of 10.
The Kraft Group did not yet provide information about possible tenants of the data center. But they’re making a bet based on the plans of AI giants like OpenAI and Anthropic, which are expected to spend hundreds of billions of dollars leasing space in such facilities.
Given the forecasts of exploding AI usage, businesses eventually will need nearby data centers to avoid software slowdowns, Eastwood said. “You’ll end up with an AI infrastructure that’s much more distributed and not as centralized,” he said, with a handful of megasized data centers needed in New England.
In parts of the country with numerous data centers, the facilities appear to have driven up electricity rates . The Sutton campus, if fully built, would draw power equal to about 7 percent of the state’s peak usage on the hottest summer day last year.
For the town of Sutton, which is struggling to balance its budget over the next few years, property tax revenue from the data center could win over skeptics.
The full facility would represent a multiple of the $2.8 billion in assessed value of all the property in Sutton, Cyganiewicz wrote.
The first two buildings on the data center campus would pay $10.4 million annually in property taxes starting in fiscal year 2031. That sum would rise to about $27.8 million a year on all 10 buildings in 2035, Cyganiewicz estimated in his letter.
In a town with a $40 million annual budget, that would be a huge windfall, potentially cutting property tax bills for residents by thousands of dollars. An average single-family homeowner in 2031 could see their tax bill fall to $6,846 from $9,134, according to Cyganiewicz.
Still, “the proposal is tentative,” he wrote. “No application has been filed, and important details on power, water, equipment and site impacts are still to come.”
The proposal was previously reported by MassLive.
Data centers have become increasingly controversial as critics point to their environmental impacts, energy consumption, and broader concerns about the effect of artificial intelligence on the job market. Governor Maura Healey in September signed an executive order to block new data centers in Massachusetts unless they get local approval.
US Representative Jim McGovern, whose district includes Sutton, has been a leading opponent of data centers and cosponsored a bill to impose a national moratorium. But McGovern said it would be up to residents to decide whether to move forward with the Kraft proposal.
“Costs of utilities have gone up for a lot of people because the data centers eat up a lot of energy and take a lot of water ... so for me, I don’t like them,” he said. “But, ultimately, it’s up to the people of Sutton.”
Nearly across the board during the midterms, pro-data center candidates backed by Big Tech, including Senate candidates Jon Husted in Ohio and Ken Paxton in Texas, lost.
Many House candidates supporting AI and data centers came up short, too, including Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin and Rob Bresnahan in Pennsylvania. And in dozens of local referendums around the country, from Wells, Maine, to Defiance, Ohio, and Emporia, Kans., voters approved bans or restrictions on data centers.
Jim Puzzanghera of the Globe staff contributed reporting.
Aaron Pressman can be reached at aaron.pressman@globe.com . Follow him @ampressman . Travis Andersen can be reached at travis.andersen@globe.com .

articles.title_orig: Windows 11 KB5132061 KB5131087 November 2026 Patch Tuesday direct download links here
articles.title_zh: Windows 11 KB5132061 KB5131087 November 2026 Patch Tuesday direct download links here
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft is investigating reports of Windows 11 KB5132061 installation errors, including 0x800f0993, 0x80070306, and 0x800f0989. In our tests, we observed that the November 2026 Patch Tuesday update reaches 99% before it fails, and you won’t make any progress even if you reattempt the installation.
On November 10, Microsoft rolled out Windows 11 KB5132061 as part of this month’s Patch Tuesday cycle, which means it’s a mandatory security update with close to 700 critical Windows-specific security fixes, plus other improvements like a customizable right-click menu.
KB5132061 bumps Windows 11 26H2 to Build 26300.9974 and 25H2 to Build 26200.9974, and it’s supposed to take a few minutes to finish installing. Usually, a Windows update requires a single reboot, but this one may require two or more reboots because of a pending Windows Secure Boot certificate update.
Two or more reboots aren’t exactly a problem, but there’s a bug that’s preventing the November 2026 update from installing. On my PC, the update installed within a few minutes. But some users aren’t even able to get it to finish installing, and retrying doesn’t help.
“I’m stuck in a loop of installing KB5132061, but it’s repeatedly throwing errors such as 0x800f0993, 0x80070306, and 0x800f0989,” one user told Windows Latest, and there are dozens of similar complaints.
One user told us that the November 2026 update failed on four of their PCs with either 0x800f0989 or 0x80070306. They tried downloading the update manually and resetting Windows Update components, but it still failed.
Another user ran into 0x80070306 on two virtual machines and shared the following error:
“Installation Failure: Windows failed to install the following update with error 0x80070306: 2026-11 Security Update (KB5132061) (26300.9974).”
I’ve also seen reports of Windows 11 KB5132061 failing with 0x800f0993 and 0x800f0922. One person said it failed seven times, including once when they tried the offline installer from the Microsoft Update Catalog, before it finally installed on another attempt.
Of course, not everyone is affected. Some users have reported that the update installed without any errors, while others say it eventually went through after they restarted their PC and tried again.
Microsoft’s support document still says the company is “not currently aware of any issues with this update.” However, that doesn’t mean Microsoft isn’t looking at the reports, as I’ve been told the company is fully aware of the complaints and is investigating the root cause, including the possibility that Sandbox is responsible.
Windows Latest understands that Windows 11 KB5132061 installation issues could be tied to Windows Sandbox, so if you turn it off, you should be able to install the cumulative update without any trouble.
For those unaware, Windows Sandbox is one of the lesser-known features of Windows, and it lets you run apps in an isolated environment (virtual machine), with the idea of easily testing untrusted programs or downloads. It’s a great addition, and some might have turned on the feature without even realizing it, and now it’s causing the November 2026 update to fail.
One user who looked at their Windows installation logs noticed an error referring to a file used by Sandbox. On their PC, the update failed while Sandbox was enabled, but installed after they turned it off and restarted.
However, I’ve also seen a report from someone who ran into the error without having the option enabled. But if you use Sandbox and the update keeps failing, it might be worth trying:
If you just can’t get Windows 11 KB5132061 to install, you can also try downloading the update from the Microsoft Update Catalog .
If nothing else works, Windows 11 has a Fix problems using Windows Update option under Settings > System > Recovery . It’ll reinstall your current version of Windows while keeping your apps, files, and settings.
For now, Microsoft is looking into the reports, and we’ll update this article when we learn more.
Mayank Parmar is an entrepreneur who founded Windows Latest. He is the Editor-in-Chief and has written on various topics in his seven years of career, but he is mostly known for his well-researched work on Microsoft's Windows. His articles and research works have been referred to by CNN, Business Insiders, Forbes, Fortune, CBS Interactive, Microsoft and many others over the years.

articles.title_orig: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
articles.title_zh: China’s Nvidia Honeypot Isn’t Surprising. Jensen Huang Fell for It Anyway
articles.content_orig:
There’s a specific mantra drilled into government workers, military officers, and intelligence personnel during counterintelligence briefings: “If she’s a 10 and you’re a 5, she’s a spy!” Or, as the US Army’s Counterintelligence Command posted on Valentine’s Day: “It doesn’t take a mathematician to figure out ‘10 + 5 = honeytrap.’” The very beautiful woman who is suddenly interested in your very ordinary existence probably has ulterior motives , is the message.
Jensen Huang surely doesn’t live a typical life—he’s a centibillionaire, the swashbuckling CEO of Nvidia, one of the hottest and most geopolitically consequential companies of the 21st century. Surely he’s aware of the possibility that he’d cross paths with intelligence assets. In fact, it’s hard to think of many companies in the world that would be a higher priority target for foreign intelligence agencies.
All of that makes the stock-shaking news this week all the more surprising. How did Huang get embroiled in a spy scandal that mixes infidelity, international espionage, the Trump administration, and the economic behemoth of the multitrillion-dollar AI industry?
The story kicked off just before Halloween, with a six-byline story in The New York Times reporting that Huang was the target of a Chinese spy plot. Starting somewhere between 2024 and 2025, Huang allegedly had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), a one-time executive at a Singapore-based cloud provider known as Megaspeed. US intelligence agencies warned top US officials that they believed she was a Chinese intelligence asset. So far, Nvidia’s board, which has launched its own investigation, says it has “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised,” but that’s far from the only concern.
As one would expect, China has denied any nefarious plot centered on Jensen Huang. A Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson on Monday said , “The narrative about so-called Chinese spies is entirely based on groundless speculation—it’s nothing more than slander and smearing.”
But according to reporting by The New York Times and the Financial Times , US intelligence officials also claim that Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was reporting to China’s Ministry of State Security intelligence agency. On Monday, Megaspeed said on LinkedIn that US authorities found “no evidence of any violations concerning the illicit transfer of chips or any illegal activities." (There’s no indication so far that Alice Huang, a one-time Chinese state journalist, is an employee or “officer” of Chinese intelligence; she’s believed to be an “asset,” an outsider who aids an intelligence agency, sometimes for pay, sometimes not.)
China, though, has elevated economic espionage to a core pillar of its economic and military development, stealing the designs for everything from US fighter jets to solar panels and commercial paint recipes . “Honeypots” or “honey traps”—positioning an alluring operative to seduce or develop a relationship with a key target—are one of intelligence’s most infamous and well-established strategies. French officials have warned specifically about Chinese honeypots since at least 2011, when intelligence reports cited a pharmaceutical researcher who was seduced and then blackmailed by a Chinese spy operation.
Over the past quarter of a century, as Silicon Valley emerged as a center of political and economic power, it has become a key focus of Chinese intelligence. In one plot, a Chinese national named Fang Fang spent years trying to cozy up to Bay Area politicians , including then US Representative Eric Swalwell. (While intelligence officials at the time reportedly believed Fang to be an operative, law enforcement officials never brought any charges against her). When traveling to China, US business executives have become accustomed to leaving their regular phones and computers at home and using burner devices to prevent the installation of spyware or malware (as I did, when I traveled to China for WIRED in 2019 to report on Huawei ). In 2012, when Leon Panetta was making his first trip to China as defense secretary, he and his team were advised to bathe and shower in the dark in the event his hotel room was bugged. Last year, the threat of honeypots prompted the US government to explicitly ban personnel working in China and Hong Kong from engaging in romantic or sexual relationships with Chinese citizens. More recently, US officials joined with allies to warn about China’s increasingly sophisticated “ LinkedIn espionage ”: using the business-focused social networking site to recruit and build relationships with unwitting executives.
Alice Huang’s Megaspeed, for its part, is a major Pacific region player in cloud services focused on the advanced computer chips that are the heart of Nvidia’s business. The Biden administration had sharply limited the export of cutting-edge chips globally to slow China’s development of AI, but Jensen Huang has successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen those restrictions.
Speaking at a press conference on Monday, Donald Trump denied having prior knowledge of Alice Huang’s potential espionage. “I didn’t hear about it then, but a lot of people have heard about it, and Jensen totally denies that,” Trump said . “I asked him that question: ‘Did you have any idea that she was a spy?’ He said, ‘I had no idea that she was a spy.’” On Tuesday, the Times reported that Marco Rubio had briefed Trump in May, right before Jensen Huang joined the President on Air Force One for a trip to China.
The veracity of Trump's claims will surely be investigated, especially in the context of the famous Watergate maxim: “What did the president know and when did he know it?” Nvidia’s CEO has been publicly linked to the Megaspeed executive since at least 2024 and Alice’s husband, Kang Weigh, has reportedly known Jensen since the 2010s. WIRED’s Lauren Goode reported on Monday that Jensen Huang, starting in 2025, hired Risa Heller’s crisis communications firm, which is well-versed in handling public sex scandals. This spring, secretary of state Marco Rubio evidently helped craft a classified memo inside the administration warning officials about Jensen Huang’s potentially compromising relationship.
Jensen Huang—who has developed an important reputation as AI’s #1 cheerleader at the frontier of AI labs—is now stuck in an awkward situation. Is he an idiot, unaware that his paramour might have been a foreign intelligence asset? Merely reckless with his own reputation, fiduciary responsibility to Nvidia, and the technological security of the United States? Or a witting accomplice to undermining US national security?
Regardless of the truth, Nvidia loses. Shareholders have ridden a roller-coaster that has seen Nvidia’s stock rise by about 600 percent over the past five years, becoming the world’s second-most valuable company. In the past month, the stock has plummeted by a quarter. The disaster for Nvidia is just beginning, it seems, as lawsuits loom, including by its own shareholders.
Similarly, the Trump administration is likely to face real questions from the newly Democratic congress: When were the president and other top officials briefed about this intelligence threat? What communication, if any, did they make to Nvidia and to whom? Should more have been done by US intelligence to block Alice Huang from having access to Nvidia and its CEO?
The fact that Megaspeed is a major customer of Nvidia makes everything more complicated. Indeed, reports have circulated for at least a year that the US was concerned that Megaspeed was diverting chips to Chinese intelligence agencies, an allegation that could have massive consequences for the global AI race. articles.title_orig: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.title_zh: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
articles.content_orig:
Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.
Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.
However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon.
Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest."
"I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible.
Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said.
After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky.
The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.
For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member.
For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.
Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.
That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence.
Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin.
Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them.
Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.
Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.
Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.
There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.
Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.
Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security.
Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.
Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.
Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again.
"These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

articles.title_orig: JetBlue unveils new first class seats to bring back profits
articles.title_zh: JetBlue unveils new first class seats to bring back profits
articles.content_orig:
JetBlue Airways is unveiling its new domestic first-class seats Wednesday as more of the country's carriers bet on the premium travel boom to make them profitable again.
JetBlue announced it would offer a domestic first class — BlueFirst — in December 2024 and plans to start flying aircraft with the new seats and full on-board product next month. The carrier is showing off the new cabin at its home hub at John F. Kennedy International Airport on Wednesday. Retrofits will continue during 2027, CEO Joanna Geraghty told CNBC late last month.
The rollout comes as the New York airline tries to stabilize after last posting a profit in 2019. Last month, JetBlue executives sought to calm investors after shares in the airline hit a record low following a report that bondholders had contracted restructuring advisors.
"We have no intention, no plans to file for bankruptcy. We are not engaged with any restructuring company," Geraghty told CNBC in an interview on Oct. 27.
Geraghty told CNBC's Phil LeBeau on Wednesday that JetBlue has "met with a few of the creditors over the last couple of weeks as part of ... normal investor engagement." She said the company made it clear to bondholders that JetBlue doesn't need to reorganize.
The airline's shares are up more than 40% this month, more than other passenger carriers, as of midday Wednesday, though they are still off about 11% so far this year.
JetBlue is betting that resilient travel demand, especially for for roomier seats will help fuel its turnaround plan, which aims to get the carrier to an operating profit next year and $1 in adjusted earnings per share in 2028.
Airline executives have said they expect fares to stay elevated next year as they grapple with higher costs, including but not limited to fuel, such as labor and airport fees. Geraghty said Wednesday that even if fuel prices moderate next year, "I don't think fares are going to fall as much as people expect."
Airlines large and small are racing to outfit their cabins with roomier, more expensive seating options to help cover ever-higher costs, from jet fuel to labor to airport operation fees.
For example, a ticket in the new recliner first-class seats between Kennedy Airport and Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida is going for $847 roundtrip in the first week of March while standard economy is $446.
On Tuesday, budget carrier Frontier Airlines unveiled its new first class seats, which will take up the first two rows, and said it would outfit its Airbus fleet with premium seating that have extra legroom and in-seat power through row eight. The airline will take out a row of seating on its planes to make the pricier ones fit, chief marketing officer Bobby Schroeter told CNBC in an interview Monday.
JetBlue last month reported it ended the third quarter with $2.2 billion in liquidity and that its unencumbered asset base is now $7 billion, including $2.8 billion in aircraft and engines.
JetBlue had total debt of $8.4 billion as of Sept. 30, the carrier said in its earnings filing.
Geraghty told CNBC last month there is a "fundamental disconnect between the narrative in the bond market and what our financial results actually demonstrate."
When asked then whether JetBlue's eye on keeping costs down includes furloughs, layoffs or buyouts, Geraghty last month said "absolutely not."

articles.title_orig: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
articles.title_zh: Google’s AlphaGenome 2 zooms in on the cellular roots of disease
articles.content_orig:
DeepMind’s new DNA model better predicts how mutations affect different cells, potentially opening paths to treatment.
DeepMind’s new DNA model better predicts how mutations affect different cells, potentially opening paths to treatment.
Researchers at Google DeepMind have unveiled a new AI model designed to unravel how changes in our DNA affect different cells, giving scientists a more detailed view of a notoriously difficult problem that could hold important clues to the causes of disease — and point the way to new treatments.
AlphaGenome 2 is the successor to DeepMind’s genome-predicting AI model AlphaGenome, which was released last year . While nearly every cell in the human body carries the same DNA, different types of cells — from heart muscle cells and skin cells to immune cells fighting an infection — switch different genes on and off, and those patterns can change depending on what a cell is doing. As a result, the same genetic variant can have very different effects depending on the type and state of the cell.
The new model is designed to capture those differences, predicting the effects of genetic variants on individual cell types and states. Google said in a blog post published Wednesday that it offers a much finer-grained view than broader models like AlphaGenome, potentially revealing disease-relevant effects in specific cells that might otherwise go unnoticed.
AlphaGenome 2 was trained on more than 100 million individual cell profiles across 68 tissues to give it that more detailed view. DeepMind says the model effectively turns static cell atlases — huge data repositories that map and catalog individual cells in detail — “into a predictive engine for human genetics.” According to the company, AlphaGenome 2 identifies nearly twice as many variants that can change gene expression in cells than its previous state-of-the-art model.
Notably, the researchers found that AlphaGenome 2 could also make predictions about new types of cells and biological states without needing to be retrained. It could also identify gaps in experimental data, potentially helping scientists decide what to investigate next in the lab.
For Adam Gayoso, a research scientist at Google DeepMind involved in the project, the big breakthrough is “tying human genetics to cell biology.” AlphaGenome 2 gives researchers a way to drill down on genetic variants identified in large populations, to see what effects they may be having on a cellular level, and potentially connect those effects to disease, he told The Verge .
Google DeepMind’s genomics lead Žiga Avsec told The Verge that this specificity is important if you have a goal like figuring out how to treat a particular disease. “When you develop drugs, you’re targeting specific proteins and specific cell types,” he explained, which makes having this kind of granularity vital.
Building a model like AlphaGenome 2 has only recently become possible thanks to new technologies that can capture individual cells and their states at high resolution and create the vast datasets needed to train it, Avsec said. DeepMind is now working to improve its genetics models by generating more data, including for cell states that aren’t represented well today. Avsec said future versions could also potentially be trained on data “across multiple species,” giving the models a broader view of biology. Longer term, he said models like AlphaGenome 2 could feed into efforts to create “ virtual cells ,” digital simulations designed to mimic biological systems.
Although Avsec said he views AlphaGenome 2 as a successor to AlphaGenome, it isn’t replacing it any time soon. He said its more detailed predictions come at a computational cost and are “more expensive” to produce than those of its predecessor, he said. Those demands would have made it impractical to use AlphaGenome 2 to produce the genome-wide Atlas covering “every possible DNA letter change in the human genome” that DeepMind released in September.
Google says it is making AlphaGenome 2 available for non-commercial research via the AlphaGenome API from today, with a limited “private preview” for commercial research.
The model is the latest in a growing array of efforts by Google and rival AI labs to use the technology to tackle major problems in science and medicine. Pushmeet Kohli, who heads DeepMind’s AI for science research, has hinted that more impressive scientific results are on the way, and the organization is expected to open an automated materials science lab in the UK soon. Anthropic, meanwhile, has been experimenting with drug design and given Claude a wet lab , while OpenAI has been mowing down an impressive amount of longstanding problems in mathematics and related fields .

articles.title_orig: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.title_zh: Kidnapper, 74, escapes from house arrest in Argentina by abseiling from balcony
articles.content_orig:
A 74-year-old Italian man who was found guilty of a kidnapping carried out by a far-left militant group in the 1970s has escaped while under house arrest in Argentina and is on the run.
Leonardo Bertulazzi used a harness to abseil down from a fifth-floor balcony in the capital, Buenos Aires.
His escape was not immediately registered because he had tampered with his electronic ankle monitor so that it continued to transmit body temperature measurements even after he had prised it open and absconded.
Bertulazzi already spent decades as a fugitive after he was sentenced in absentia in Italy for the 1977 kidnapping of Italian naval engineer Pietro Costa.
He was awaiting extradition to Italy and was being monitored by the Argentine ministry of security through an ankle tag which registers the wearer's body temperature and movements.
Officials said that they had become suspicious when they noticed that the tag had remained stationary.
When they entered the fifth-floor apartment in the centre of Buenos Aires, Bertulazzi was gone, but the ankle monitor remained.
Wary of Bertulazzi's past with the Marxist guerilla group the Red Brigades and his bomb-making skills, police called in explosives experts in case it had been rigged to detonate, according to Argentine newspaper Clarín.
However, the experts found that while Bertulazzi had tampered with the device, he had done so to prevent the alarm from sounding once he removed it.
A nationwide manhunt is now under way.
Italian media say that his extradition to Italy had been imminent after his last appeal was rejected.
Bertulazzi was first arrested after using a false passport to cross into Argentina from neighbouring Chile in 2002.
However, he was granted refugee status in 2004 and lived freely in the South American country until his re-arrest in 2024, when the current right-wing president, Javier Milei, took office.
Milei's government said at the time that "Bertulazzi is responsible for crimes that undermined democratic values and the lives of many victims".
He was a member of the Red Brigades, which kidnapped and killed a number of state officials in the 1970s and '80s.
Bertulazzi was part of the Red Brigades' Genoa section that kidnapped Pietro Costa on the street and then held him for 81 days before receiving a big ransom.
The money it made from the kidnapping was then used to buy a flat in Rome, which was used in 1978 for the Red Brigades' most notorious crime, the kidnap and murder of Italian former Prime Minister, Aldo Moro.
Moro was abducted when his car was ambushed on the way to the opening of parliament. He was held in the flat for 54 days before he was shot and his body abandoned in the boot of a Renault car in the centre of Rome.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia Scandal Puts Lori Huang, Jensen Huang’s Wife, In the Spotlight
articles.title_zh: Nvidia Scandal Puts Lori Huang, Jensen Huang’s Wife, In the Spotlight
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia 's stock rose 3% on Wednesday, after falling for two days amid the scandal that has rocked the world's most valuable tech company.
Shares closed down 5.47% on Tuesday as more details were revealed about the impact of CEO Jensen Huang 's affair with an alleged Chinese spy . They fell 4.3% Monday.
On Tuesday, Nvidia announced it had hired law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to investigate whether company secrets or national security were compromised.
Huang tried to project "business as usual" as he returned to the office on Monday, people familiar with the matter told CNBC. The CEO was also in the office on Tuesday, conducting meetings, ahead of the company's quarterly earnings on Nov. 17.
Investors are assessing whether the matter will have damaging spillover effects on the business.
In a Tuesday note, Bank of America said it saw three scenarios with differing investment outcomes. In one scenario, the impact is contained with leadership continuity, and in another, prolonged uncertainty pressures valuation before earnings.
In the final scenario, the impact is escalated, with "adverse findings, leadership disruption or tighter restrictions requiring earnings reassessment," BofA research analyst Vivek Arya said in the note.
Zacks' Chief Equity Strategist John Blank said the selloff reflected two concerns: that the U.S. might impose further restrictions in the wake of the affair and that further problems might arise as the news develops. "What else has Jensen done?" he said.
"It's not good for Nvidia. It's not good for Jensen Huang. It's certainly not good for the AI trade," Blank told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Wednesday.
Morgan Stanley on Wednesday removed Nvidia as a top pick after shares dropped more than 25% since it was named on the list on Oct. 2. Huang's leadership is "crucial" to the company's strategic direction, analysts said in a Wednesday note.
— CNBC's Michael Bloom and Caleigh Keating contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.title_zh: Pope Leo returns to Peru, his adopted homeland
articles.content_orig:
Lee el artículo en español
Riding on horseback to visit the most isolated Andean areas of his community, distributing food amid the Covid-19 pandemic, or wearing rubber boots in the water and mud of floods: this is how many Peruvians remember the man who is now Pope Leo XIV.
Robert Prevost was in the trenches and alongside his people during Peru’s most difficult moments, and many of these memories will likely be front of mind among the public as they welcome the pope on his visit to his adopted homeland on Wednesday.
The pope’s visit to Peru, which will include visits to Lima, Cusco and Chiclayo, is widely seen as a homecoming for a pontiff who is a Peruvian citizen and who knows the country in depth.
A young Prevost first arrived in the South American country as a missionary in 1985. The years that followed shaped his leadership style, which would later lead him to become the successor to the late Pope Francis.
“I think he was heroic in many ways; he risked becoming ill. We lost 11 priests and a bishop emeritus during that time,” Father José Del Rosario recalls of the most difficult days of the pandemic.
Padre Robert, as he is known in Spanish in Peru, traveled more than 700 kilometers (435 miles) from Chiclayo to the Diocese of Callao, a province bordering the capital, Lima, where he served as apostolic administrator.
“He came every two weeks in his little car; he came alone in a simple pickup truck,” explained Del Rosario, parish priest and rector of the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Mount Carmel of La Legua, who worked closely with the then-bishop.
Pope! Amigo! Peruvians remember the young American priest who became pope
Prevost distributed food and everything needed by a population that lived under lockdown for months, while also offering spiritual guidance during the crisis.
“He gave us a lot of hope and cared for our people, a man who was very close to the people … and also very humble,” Del Rosario added.
Peru recorded more than 219,000 deaths , according to Johns Hopkins University figures, and one of the highest coronavirus mortality rates in the world. In Lima, and especially in the regions, terrifying scenes unfolded outside hospitals, with sick people collapsing in the street due to the shortage of oxygen, one of the key tools for treating the virus.
In Chiclayo, Bishop Prevost launched a fundraising campaign to purchase an oxygen plant. Together with Caritas Chiclayo, the bishop appealed to authorities and sectors of civil society and managed to raise more than US$380,000 for not just one but two oxygen plants.
Janinna Sesa, former director of Caritas Chiclayo, worked with the bishop for eight years, including during the pandemic, the flooding caused by the coastal El Niño in 2017, and Cyclone Yaku in 2023.
“We were always on the front lines, especially during disasters like the coastal El Niño phenomenon. He was the person who put on his boots and waded into the water; he helped people. He was very approachable and very kind,” Sesa told CNN.
Before leaving for Rome in 2023, after the late Pope Francis appointed him prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, Bishop Prevost also led appeals for aid for the more than 10,000 people affected by flooding caused by Cyclone Yaku in the north of the country.
“I ask you to be generous; I ask you to open your hearts so that we can help one another and move forward, as we have done in other times of crisis,” Prevost said in a video while standing in the water in the district of Illimo, in the Lambayeque region.
The assistance and response led by Prevost in the face of the massive arrival of Venezuelan migrants in 2018 was comprehensive and had a different vision from that of the country’s other regions.
Peru received more than 1.6 million Venezuelans through November 2025, the second-highest number in the region after Colombia. More than 20,000 of them passed through Chiclayo, and more than 3,500 families settled in the region, according to figures from the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking of the Diocese of Chiclayo. Prevost also promoted this commission to assist migrants and combat human trafficking.
First American pope marks July 4 on migrant island with plea for ‘compassion and generosity’
“The migration flow descended upon us, with thousands of migrants out on the streets, sleeping there, and the parishes serving as shelters,” Sesa recalled.
Father Robert was concerned not only with providing food and collecting clothing, blankets, and medicine, but also with building the San Vicente de Paúl village, which took them in at Puerto Etén.
“His simplicity, the peace he conveys, that serenity Monsignor Prevost had when listening to people — I still see it in Pope Leo XIV…. He welcomed us with such warmth, with so much love,” Lisbeth Díaz, a Venezuelan resident of Chiclayo and member of the Commission for Human Mobility and Human Trafficking, told CNN.
Prevost prioritized regularizing their legal status so they could work and integrate into society.
Prevost created spaces for dialogue and encouraged many people to raise their voices to denounce abuses during the internal conflict the country experienced beginning in the 1980s and to openly discuss the social reality during the authoritarian regime of the late President Alberto Fujimori in the 1990s.
At the Augustinian mission in Trujillo, the current pontiff and his seminarians traveled through towns and parishes in Andean areas, staging dramatizations that reflected the violence faced by peasants to encourage conversations that would help heal the trauma and pain they had suffered.
Prevost also participated in collecting signatures for the creation of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission (TRC), which investigated the violence between 1980 and 2000 and human rights abuses, particularly in rural Peru. Trujillo and the parishes led by the current pontiff collected the largest number of signatures.
Leo XIV is a pope forged in Peru. The nearly two decades he spent in the land he adopted as his own profoundly shaped his ministry and set him on the path to the papacy. As a bishop, Prevost was a pastor close to his flock, and at the Vatican, one of his closest collaborators is the Reverend Edgard Rimaycuna, a native of Chiclayo.
His work in South America and his leadership of the Order of Saint Augustine caught the attention of Pope Francis, who first appointed him bishop of Chiclayo and later brought him to Rome, where he went on to hold one of the most important positions in the Vatican and also became a cardinal. This made him a candidate in the 2025 conclave.
Pope Leo presides at biggest Mass of his papacy in Buenos Aires, drawing 2.5 million crowd
In the past, the election of an American pope was considered impossible, given that the College of Cardinals did not wish to associate the papacy with the dominant political and cultural power. However, the cardinals who voted for Cardinal Robert Prevost in the 2025 conclave did not see him simply as a candidate from the United States.
His experience in Peru garnered broad consensus among the cardinals, who chose a bishop with roots in Latin America — someone who speaks Spanish fluently and is attuned to the concerns of the people of that continent.
The pope’s visit to Peru will be an opportunity for the Peruvian people to welcome Padre Robert back to the adopted country that shaped him — and that he shaped deeply as well.
Reverend John Lydon, a priest and member of the same Augustinian religious order to which the pope belongs, and who lived and worked with Prevost for a decade, told CNN: “I believe his dedication to the poor and his defense of human rights will continue to define his visit.”

articles.title_orig: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
articles.title_zh: If you bought an iPhone Duo, have you kept or returned it? [Poll]
articles.content_orig:
When Apple announced the iPhone Duo back in September, the company called it “the most transformational change to iPhone since the original,” and there’s no doubt that it generated a huge amount of excitement.
But a new report suggests that for some buyers the novelty quickly wore off, and they ended up returning their devices. Is this just a handful of people, or is it more common … ?
It’s been a very long time since any smartphone launch has generated quite so much buzz. Apple called it a breakthrough in iPhone design.
iPhone Duo features a breakthrough foldable design that’s beautiful, versatile, and durable, opening up possibilities that feel entirely new yet remarkably familiar […]
“iPhone Duo is the most transformational change to iPhone since the original. With an entirely new design and intuitive experiences, it shows what’s possible when hardware and software are engineered together and redefines what it means to use a foldable phone,” said John Ternus.
Despite not really being the target market for the phone, I was still wowed by the launch video and remained incredibly impressed when I got some hands-on time with one.
Many couldn’t resist buying one despite the price – but The Verge notes that not everyone has ending up keeping the device. Apple allows you to return any product within 14 days for a full refund without having to give any reason. That window has come to an end for some of the first buyers and the site’s Alison Johnson spoke with some of those who’d decided to take advantage of it.
The iPhone Duo replaced both my iPhone 15 Pro Max and my iPad Mini 6. It now is my phone and iPad mini in my pocket. This is the dream phone I never knew I wanted.
And for the lack of Face ID, Touch ID works perfect with my Apple Watch. And even without wearing it, I don’t see the big deal of the ‘huge’ effort of bringing my finger to a button.
For the lacking 5x zoom that I had on my Pro Max, I haven’t had a moment yet that I wanted to use it to be honest. Those moments will definitely arise, but the lack of that camera cannot go up against the amazing overall experience of the iPhone Duo.
There were a few specific issues:
But the more fundamental reason for some is that it hasn’t really lived up to their hopes for a multifunctional device.
“If I can have an iPad in my pocket, that would be great.” So thought Ben Seligson, a content creator, photographer, and now former iPhone Duo owner […] “Usually I’d throw a YouTube video on the iPad or throw a podcast up. And then I start cooking dinner and leave my iPad in one spot, but I’d have my phone in my pocket if I got a text, or I needed to set a timer or something like that.” With the Duo, the phone was also the iPad on the counter, so a quick reply became much more of an interruption.
I’m curious as to whether this is just a small minority of buyers or a more common phenomenon. If you bought a Duo early enough to have hit the end of the return window, please take our poll to let us know whether you decided to keep it or return it – and do share your reasons in the comments (which are now back).
Oh, and the good news for anyone buying one now is that you’ll have a lot longer to make up your mind, with the extended return window for the holidays in place. You can now return anything bought today through January 8.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of hoax bomb alerts sent to schools in Italy, U.K. and Ireland
articles.title_zh: Thousands of hoax bomb alerts sent to schools in Italy, U.K. and Ireland
articles.content_orig:
Schools across Italy were evacuated on Wednesday ⁠after around 6,300 of them received bomb warnings, the latest in a series of threats and cyberattacks around Europe against supermarkets , blood banks, air traffic and broadcasters.
Scotland, Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland said many of their schools received a similar email threat from abroad but it was classed as a hoax and did not disrupt classes.
In Italy, schools closed swiftly after ⁠the warnings, prompting many parents to drop what they were ​doing ⁠to collect children.
“My daughter Dafne started crying because the kids did not understand what was happening, and she was still shaken when I picked her up,” said Nensi Bego, parent of a child ⁠at the Mazzini middle school in Rome.
“This is so annoying. It’s obvious it’s just a hoax that disrupts ​lessons and ⁠disrupts everyone’s day.”
A copy of the ‌message seen by Reuters also included a threat to target Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni . She said the bomb alerts posed no danger and that police and other public bodies were monitoring the situation.
“All students have been taken ‌to a safe area and remain under the supervision of teaching ‌staff,” one school in Rome informed parents through a messaging app.
The email received in Italy was signed “Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan,” according to a copy of the message seen by Reuters.
“The (school) emails are public. (Sending the bomb alert messages) was as easy as drinking a ⁠glass of water,” a national security source told Reuters.
The same purported author claimed responsibility for email bomb threats sent on Friday to newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria.
Some European officials suspect Russia may be behind a campaign of disruption to everyday life in European nations supporting Ukraine after Moscow’s invasion.
Russia denies that and accuses the West of a smear campaign.
Iran is another suspect. France summoned Iran’s ambassador on Tuesday after accusing Tehran of a cyberattack that disabled refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets last week.
Iran rejected those accusations as “baseless and hostile”.
Italian ‌Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said Wednesday’s threats were part of a clear strategy “to spread fear and ​create anxiety,” according to Adnkronos news agency.
“It is not always the work of foreign countries ‌or hostile entities. There are also attention-seekers and lunatics ⁠who, at a time like this, cannot wait to unleash terror in a city or a region,” ⁠he added.
Antonello Giannelli, head of the Italian School Principals Association, said the alerts were upsetting for students, families and school staff.
“Even though today’s ‌threats are clearly hoaxes, we cannot underestimate ​the consequences of incidents that alarm entire school communities ‌and disrupt the normal conduct of educational activities,” he ​said.

articles.title_orig: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.title_zh: Egyptian journalist's retrial adjourned as UN warns of 'assaults on press freedom'
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Six journalists who make up the entire newsroom of the Egyptian fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention, the UN human rights office (OHCHR) said on Tuesday, warning of proliferating assaults on press freedom by the Government.
“ We are witnessing widening assaults on press freedom by Egyptian authorities, including the targeting, persecution and harassment of independent journalists ,” the human rights chief’s spokesperson Thameen Al-Kheetan told journalists in Geneva.
“ These alarming developments must end immediately , and journalists must be able to carry out their essential work free from intimidation and reprisals.”
The detained reporters are Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Abdallah Qadry, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel. According to their lawyers, they were tortured and otherwise ill-treated and forced to record fabricated confessions.
Lina Attalah, chief editor of the independent online news outlet Mada Masr, also faces continuing judicial harassment linked to her journalistic work, the OHCHR spokesperson said.
Last month, an Egyptian court convicted her of operating an unlicensed website. She was detained, then released after paying a fine, and the court ordered the website closed.
This week, she faces another hearing in a separate case dating back to 2024 – raising fresh concerns over legal due process and the right to a fair trial, including obstacles to appeal.
OHCHR called on Egypt to end all forms of harassment of journalists and media outlets, and to respect and fulfil the right to freedom of expression, including the right to information.
The authorities must release all the Matsadash reporters and drop charges arising from their legitimate journalistic work, the UN rights office said. Until then, they must have confidential access to lawyers, contact with their families, necessary healthcare and medication, and humane conditions of detention .
“ All allegations of torture, ill-treatment or forced confessions must be promptly investigated, and those responsible held to account ,” Mr. Al-Kheetan said.
The office also called for the measures taken to suppress the work of both Matsadash and Mada Masr to be overturned.
“The people of Egypt have a right to read and hear views expressed through these fora on issues of legitimate public concern.”
Alessandra Vellucci, Director of the UN Information Service in Geneva, recalled the Secretary-General’s message on the International Day to End Impunity for Crimes against Journalists on 2 November.

articles.title_orig: Four bears killed in Canada after attack on mother and daughter
articles.title_zh: Four bears killed in Canada after attack on mother and daughter
articles.content_orig:
Four grizzly bears have been killed in connection with a fatal attack on a mother and daughter in the Canadian province of British Columbia.
Jennifer Balcarras, 48, and her daughter Selah Reed, 20, died earlier this month after going on an afternoon walk in a trail area in Bella Coola.
The British Columbia Conservation Office Service (BCCOS) launched an investigation into their deaths and forensic testing has since confirmed a sow and her three cubs were responsible for the attack.
All four were destroyed "in accordance with provincial human-wildlife conflict response guidelines" to protect the public, BCCOS Inspector Jeff Tyre said in an update on Tuesday.
"Evidence from the investigation as well as animal DNA was analysed and conclusively linked to a sow and its three offspring," he added.
The attack "likely involved predatory behaviour", which Tyre said was "very rare".
He added that more than a dozen conservation officers took part in the investigation over the past week, amid "difficult terrain and weather".
Balcarras and Reed were "two peas in a pod" who "got along really, really well" and shared many hobbies, Balcarras' brother, Josh, told CBC.
"When Jenny hiked, Selah was right there beside her," he said.
Tyre said DNA testing also confirmed the four bears were not involved in a 2025 attack on a school group also in the Bella Coola area.
The incident in November of last year saw 11 people injured, two of them critically, while the bear responsible was never found.
"Today, we have learned from the BC Conservation Officer Service members that they have captured and euthanized the bears involved in the recent fatal attack," said Samuel Schooner, Elected Chief of the Nuxalk Nation, in a statement.
"We would like to thank the BC Conservation Officer Service for their dedication and hard work to resolve this incident. This attack has been deeply re-triggering for our community members as we continue to recover from last year's attack. Our thoughts remain with the victims' families."

articles.title_orig: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
articles.title_zh: Fed's Goolsbee calls inflation report 'borderline disturbing' as central bank weighs more hikes
articles.content_orig:
Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee called the latest inflation data "borderline disturbing."
"It's another distressing report — borderline disturbing," Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday.
"We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Goolsbee said. "We're going to have to deal with that."
The consumer price index rose 0.4% on a seasonally adjusted basis in October, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics' Tuesday morning release. That was higher than economists had predicted, and the third straight month of outsized price increases.
Goolsbee said he had not seen drivers of prices like tariffs fade over time like he had hoped. He also said continuously high inflation on services concerned him.
And the Chicago Fed chief said lofty prices are a top issue for many people he meets.
"It's on everyone's mind," Goolsbee said. "It's on business mind. It's on nonprofits' minds. It's on ordinary consumers' mind."
Tuesday's inflation report landed at a critical juncture for the central bankers at the Federal Reserve as they considers their next interest rate move — and the moves they may have to make in the months ahead if the numbers continue to come in hot.
Goolsbee's comments arrived on the heels of remarks from other Fed officials Tuesday who said the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee may need to act more decisively to rein in inflation.
When it raises or lowers rates, the Fed typically moves by a quarter-percentage point. But Fed Governor Christopher Waller said in London early Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for an outsized half-point increase in December, and specifically said such a hike should be on the table if the core CPI, a metric that removes volatile food and energy costs, was "around 0.3." Hours later, that's exactly what happened.
Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan, speaking Tuesday after the inflation report, said she sees a need for two additional quarter-point increases, and said "it may be possible to move more rapidly this winter than the FOMC has moved so far this fall."
Anna Paulson, president of the Philadelphia Fed, was more sanguine. While she acknowledged that "inflation pressures are still very much with us," she said Tuesday that the central bank didn't need to move too quickly. "For now, further gradual tightening seems appropriate," she said. "The exact path will depend on how conditions evolve, and I'll be watching the data closely."
The committee raised rates by a quarter point in September, to a range of 3.75%-4%, before voting to hold them steady in October.
After years of higher-than-preferred price growth , Goolsbee said the possibility of consumers and businesses beginning to expect hot inflation is a "major concern." If that does happen, he said it can make the process of cooling inflation "much more painful."
But Goolsbee didn't specify whether he thought the Fed should hike rates at its December policy gathering as a result of these concerns. "I'm not a fan of being very specific and tying our hands at the next meeting or meetings in the future," Goolsbee said.
Waller, Logan and Paulson are voting members of the FOMC this year, which means they will cast votes on whether to raise rates at the committee's final meeting of the year in December. Goolsbee will be a voting member next year.
In the wake of the inflation report and the remarks from the various Fed officials, fed funds futures are now unanimously expecting a rate hike at the December meeting, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
Now the question is about whether the central bank will raise rates by a quarter or half percentage point. The fed funds futures currently put the odds of a half-point hike at the upcoming December meeting at 15%.
Odds of rates reaching 4.25%-4.5% by the January meeting — the equivalent of either a single half-point rise or two quarter-point hikes — are now at 60%, with a 10% chance of rates hitting 4.5%-4.75% by then.

articles.title_orig: Kenya's Ebola outbreak: Last patient discharged as countdown begins to be being declared free of the virus
articles.title_zh: Kenya's Ebola outbreak: Last patient discharged as countdown begins to be being declared free of the virus
articles.content_orig:
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October 2026
Kenya has discharged its last Ebola patient - the seventh to recover from the virus - marking a major milestone in efforts to contain the disease in the East African nation, which now begins a 42-day countdown to officially being declared Ebola-free.
It had confirmed its first ever case of Ebola early in October when a Kenyan businessman died within days of arriving in the capital, Nairobi.
He had contracted the virus in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where more than 5,000 people have died in an ongoing outbreak that began in May. His mother also subsequently died.
Kenya's health minister said 135 identified contacts of the infected patients had also completed their 21 days in isolation.
"Today with the discharge of the last patient we can confirm and tell the world that seven patients have recovered - and all contacts have completed their follow-up monitoring," Aden Duale said.
The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) described it as an important achievement in the regional response to the outbreak.
"This is an encouraging moment for Kenya and for Africa. We must sustain surveillance and vigilance until the outbreak is officially declared over," Africa CDC chief Jean Kaseya posted on X.
What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?
Kenya has reported no new confirmed cases since 20 October.
All the Kenyan cases were linked to the man who had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda, with health officials reporting no evidence of wider community transmission.
Those who have recovered following treatment included four healthcare workers.
Five patients were discharged on 3 November, followed by a sixth three days later, before the final patient was cleared on Wednesday.
Under World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines, 42 days must pass after the last patient tests negative and is discharged, or the last Ebola victim is safely buried, before an outbreak can be declared over.
The Ebola virus spreads through contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning those exposed to the virus may not become ill for several weeks.
Duale said the government would maintain heightened surveillance at border crossings, airports, health facilities and communities throughout the countdown.
Emergency response teams will remain on alert across the country, while the health authorities will continue monitoring travellers arriving from affected countries.
Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas are required to complete electronic health declarations before travelling, undergo screening on arrival and spend 21 days in quarantine under the supervision of health teams.
The minister also urged countries that had imposed travel and visa restrictions to reconsider them - adding that Kenya had no intention of serving as a quarantine centre for another country.
In May, a Kenyan court suspended US plans to open an Ebola quarantine facility for American citizens.
Kenya has maintained that there is no need to restrict domestic travel, trade or public gatherings.
The outbreak has nevertheless disrupted international travel, with some Gulf countries introducing restrictions affecting travellers from Kenya and other African countries.
Saudi Arabia stopped issuing visas to Kenyan nationals in late October, prompting concerns among those seeking employment there.
Meanwhile, the United Arab Emirates (UAE) has announced that it is lifting its suspension on issuing new visas to Ugandan nationals, easing restrictions introduced in June.
But Ugandans will have to spend at least 21 days outside of Uganda before being allowed to travel to the UAE.
The UAE is also allowing certain students, diplomatic passport holders and Ugandan embassy employees to enter under approved health procedures.
Uganda, which shares a long and busy border with DR Congo, was among the countries first affected but declared its own Ebola outbreak over on 27 August.
The current outbreak in DR Congo has been caused by the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, which is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.

articles.title_orig: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.title_zh: What’s the Falklands oil project at the heart of latest UK-Argentina spat?
articles.content_orig:
Lawyer says Britain wrong to believe in historic doctrine that crown has sovereignty over parts of oceans
Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici , Argentina has told an international tribunal.
Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.
Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.
Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet on Tuesday a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.
Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.
“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici ,” he said. “ We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”
Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.
She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.
Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.
The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.
Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.
In his closing remarks to the panel of 20 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.
He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”
Sam Wordsworth KC, responding for the UK, said there was nothing in the convention on the law of the seas, over which Itlos has jurisdiction, which obliged a state not to “aggravate” a sovereignty dispute and that the UN resolution cited by Kohen as the “elephant in the room” was not legally binding.
The UK further claims there is no need for urgent suspension of drilling as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an Itlos arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on Argentina’s wider claim that its rights have been breached.
During his recent speech at the UN general assembly, Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause”. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
Itlos is expected to make its ruling on Argentina’s case on 28 November.

articles.title_orig: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.title_zh: John Kerry: America Must Now Follow China’s Lead on Clean Energy
articles.content_orig:
Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’
Cop31 live – latest updates
China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels , and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.
Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.
Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.
“[China] realised suddenly they had way too much dependency on oil and gas from other places, and they decided they needed to be independent. Other countries, since the war in Iran, and since the strait of Hormuz has been interrupted, have made a similar decision, and they’re moving independently. There’s been a massive uptick in deployment of renewables. Thank you, Donald Trump.”
For autocratic states without free and fair elections , seeing the economic benefits reaped by China would be the spur to adopt low-carbon growth, he added.
“They’ll see where the market is going, and they will recognise where the cheaper alternatives are. Even they can read a spreadsheet, and understand where costs are exorbitant [in fossil fuels], and where you have a better deal,” Kerry said. “Right now, renewables together with storage, together with some transitional gas, is cheaper and more effective, than just going with fossil fuels.”
He added: “The marketplace has made its decision and globally is moving to electrons, and electrostate status. People are going to electricity and they’re going to try to do that as clean as humanly possible. That’s the choice that I see being implemented in many different places. It is unstoppable.”
China has already said it wants Cop31 to discuss the free flow of green technology against a backdrop of “intensifying” geopolitical conflicts – widely seen as a reference to US and EU tariffs on items such as Chinese electric vehicles and solar products.
Li Shuo from the Asia Society Policy Institute (ASPI) puts it this way : “In a world where climate action was once seen as a constraint on growth but is now increasingly a driver of it, China faces a singular question: will it step into a leadership role not out of obligation, but out of self-interest?”
The summit’s presidency has promised this Cop will be one of “implementation and acceleration” – and when it comes to the green transition, nowhere has implemented or accelerated quite like China. As a result, emissions have been in a “flat or falling” trend since March 2024, analysis for Carbon Brief shows .
Beijing sees the energy transition as “central to economic modernisation and energy security, with significant implications for international influence”, said Kevin Tu from the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies. The wars in Ukraine and the Middle East and their effect on oil and gas supplies have only hardened that stance.
The conflicts have also highlighted the geopolitical implications of a planetary shift to green energy. In the fossil fuel era, the designation of the US dollar as the global trading currency for oil gave Washington “what has been termed the exorbitant privilege of being the global lender of last resort”, said Isabel Hilton, the founder of the specialist environment outlet China Dialogue.
after newsletter promotion
“Without that, the US position in the world looks weaker, and if you add China’s dominance of the supply of clean technologies and the supply chains that produce them, US dominance looks more vulnerable still.”
Meanwhile, President Xi Jinping describes China as a “doer and go-getter working for the cause of global development” and state media frequently showcase Chinese renewable projects in countries ranging from Indonesia to Pakistan and Kenya. The value of the green energy deals in China’s belt and road initiative in the first half of 2026 has already surpassed the total for the whole of 2025, a recent analysis showed .
Those countries could be useful allies if China can get the subject of tariffs into the talks. “China is likely to find support from Brazil, India, South Africa and other developing countries concerned about the costs and market-access effects of climate-related trade measures,” said Tu.
China has generally held back from policy ambition or agenda-setting at forums such as Cop. Its attitude to the plans to set a global target for electrification has been ambivalent, even though it would easily hit it, according to ASPI’s Kate Logan. Partly, China has an aversion to prescriptive outside targets, but it is also trying to navigate the divergent interests of its global south partners.
Yixian Sun, a professor of sustainability governance at the University of Bath, said: “I still think there is a mismatch between Chinese policymakers’ views on the role that China can play in global climate governance and international expectations on the influence that China should exert.”
If the world wants China to play a leadership role, the environment needs to change, and more trust extended, he says. “They have to be ready to accept China’s leadership, and I don’t think this is the case, especially for global north countries”.
Analysts will watch China’s actions around climate finance commitments and support for a “just transition” – a framework designed to secure workers’ rights and livelihoods in the move away from fossil fuels.
They will also be looking for signals Beijing will bid for Cop33 in 2028; officials are said to be trying to decide if hosting would be beneficial.
For now, said Logan, “China would be happy with a Cop that doesn’t necessarily produce anything monumental, but comes out with a relatively cooperative outcome … so no major drama.”
